solution.why_others_wrong: 32 is the captain's age; 30.5 halves 61 without using the 3-year gap.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader sold a mixer-grinder at a loss of 12% for ₹1,232. At what price should he sell it to gain 15%?

solution.concept: Find the cost price first; profit and loss percentages are on the cost price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,416.80 adds 15% to the old selling price instead of the cost price; ₹1,564.64 adds 27% to the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above the cost price and allows a discount of 15% on the marked price. What is his profit percentage?

solution.explanation: Take CP = 100. MP = 140 and SP = 85% of 140 = 119, so the profit is 19%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% subtracts the discount from the markup directly (40 − 15).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer claims to sell rice at 8% above cost price, but uses a weight of 900 g in place of 1 kg. What is his actual gain percentage?

solution.concept: Dishonest dealer: gain factor = (1 + stated markup) × (true weight ÷ weight given)
solution.explanation: Let 1 g cost ₹1. He gives 900 g, costing ₹900, but charges for 1,000 g at 8% above cost, i.e. ₹1,080. Gain = 180 on 900 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18% adds 8% and 10%; 19.11% adds 8% and 11.11%; 16⅔% divides the gain of 180 by the 1,080 he charges instead of by the cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sells a scooter to B at a profit of 20%. B sells it to C at a loss of 10%. If C pays ₹59,400, at what price did A buy it?

solution.concept: Chain of transactions: multiply the factors and divide back
steps: C's price = A's CP × 1.20 × 0.90 = 1.08 × A's CP
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹54,000 treats the net change as +10% (20 − 10); ₹53,460 takes 90% of C's price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer bought 60 calculators at ₹480 each. He sold two-thirds of them at a profit of 25% and the rest at a loss of 10%. What is his overall profit percentage?

solution.concept: Overall profit is a weighted average of the individual percentages (weights = cost of each lot)
solution.explanation: 40 calculators are sold at 25% profit and 20 at 10% loss. Since each calculator costs the same, the overall profit is (2 × 25 − 1 × 10) ÷ 3 = 40/3 = 13⅓%.
solution.shortcut: Weighted average: (2 × 25 + 1 × (−10)) ÷ 3 = 13⅓%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5% is the simple average of +25% and −10%; 15% just subtracts 10 from 25.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader marks his goods 50% above cost. He allows two successive discounts of 10% each and, in addition, gives one article free with every nine articles bought. What is his overall profit percentage?

solution.concept: Successive discounts multiply; 'one free with nine' means 10 articles are given for the price of 9
solution.explanation: Take the CP of one article as 100. MP = 150; after 10% and 10%, the price is 150 × 0.81 = 121.5. For 10 articles (cost 1,000) he receives 9 × 121.5 = 1,093.5, so the profit is 9.35%.
steps: He gives 10 articles and is paid for 9: 9 × 121.5 = 1,093.5
solution.why_others_wrong: 21.5% ignores the free article; 8% adds the two discounts to 20% instead of applying them one after the other.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man bought two used laptops for ₹84,000 in total. He sold one at a profit of 16% and the other at a loss of 12%, and on the whole neither gained nor lost. What was the cost price of the laptop sold at a loss?

solution.concept: No overall gain or loss: the profit on one equals the loss on the other
solution.explanation: 16% of x = 12% of (84,000 − x), so 4x = 3(84,000 − x), giving x = ₹36,000 for the one sold at a profit. The one sold at a loss cost 84,000 − 36,000 = ₹48,000.
steps: Let the CP of the profitable laptop be x
solution.shortcut: The costs are in the inverse ratio of the percentages: 12 : 16 = 3 : 4, so 4/7 × 84,000 = 48,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹36,000 is the laptop sold at a profit; ₹42,000 assumes both cost the same.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: After allowing a discount of 18%, a store sells a pair of shoes for ₹1,968. What is the marked price?

solution.explanation: 1,968 is 82% of the marked price, so MP = 1,968 ÷ 0.82 = ₹2,400.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,322.24 adds 18% to the selling price; the discount is on the marked price, not on the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On a microwave oven marked at ₹5,000, one shop offers a flat 30% discount and another offers successive discounts of 20% and 10%. How much more does a customer pay at the second shop?

solution.concept: Successive discounts a% and b% equal a single discount of a + b − ab/100
solution.explanation: Flat 30%: 5,000 × 0.70 = ₹3,500. Successive 20% and 10%: 5,000 × 0.8 × 0.9 = ₹3,600. The second shop costs ₹100 more.
solution.shortcut: 20% and 10% successive = 28% single; 2% of 5,000 = ₹100.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No difference' assumes 20% + 10% = 30%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper allows a discount of 20% on the marked price and still makes a profit of 12%. If the cost price of an article is ₹1,500, what is its marked price?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,016 adds 20% to the selling price instead of dividing by 0.8; ₹1,980 adds 32% to the cost price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By allowing a discount of 12.5% on the marked price, a dealer earns a profit of 22.5%. What would his profit percentage be if he allowed a discount of 20% instead?

solution.concept: The ratio MP : CP stays fixed; recompute SP with the new discount
solution.explanation: MP × 0.875 = CP × 1.225, so MP = 1.4 × CP. With a 20% discount, SP = 0.8 × 1.4 × CP = 1.12 × CP: a 12% profit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% just reduces the profit by the extra 7.5% discount, ignoring that the discount is on a larger base (MP).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the simple interest on ₹12,500 at 8% per annum for 3 years and 6 months?

solution.concept: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, with T in years
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,000 ignores the 6 months; ₹16,000 is the amount, not the interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money doubles itself in 8 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become 3.5 times itself at the same rate?

solution.concept: At simple interest, the interest grows linearly with time
solution.explanation: Doubling means interest = 100% of the principal in 8 years, so the rate is 12.5% per annum. To become 3.5 times, the interest must be 250%, which takes 250 ÷ 12.5 = 20 years.
steps: Interest in 8 years = 100% of P ⇒ R = 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5%
solution.shortcut: 100% takes 8 years, so 250% takes 8 × 2.5 = 20 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 multiplies 8 by 3.5, using the amount instead of the interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum is lent at simple interest at 6% per annum for the first 2 years, 8% per annum for the next 3 years and 10% per annum after that. If the total interest at the end of 8 years is ₹7,920, find the sum.

solution.concept: With changing rates, add up rate × years for each period
solution.explanation: Total rate-years = 6 × 2 + 8 × 3 + 10 × 3 = 12 + 24 + 30 = 66, so the interest is 66% of the sum. Sum = 7,920 ÷ 0.66 = ₹12,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,375 uses the plain average rate 8% for all 8 years; ₹11,000 counts 4 years at 10%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi lent ₹40,000 in two parts: one part to Suresh at 8% per annum and the rest to Manoj at 12% per annum, both at simple interest. After 3 years he received ₹11,520 as total interest. How much did he lend to Suresh?

solution.concept: Split-sum problems: set up one equation, or use alligation on the average rate
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16,000 is the part lent to Manoj (the ratio read the wrong way round).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the compound interest on ₹15,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually.

solution.shortcut: For 2 years at 10%, CI = 21% of P = 0.21 × 15,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,000 is simple interest; ₹18,150 is the amount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 8% per annum is ₹96. Find the sum.

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,200 divides by 0.08 instead of 0.08²; ₹7,500 divides by 2 × 0.0064.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the compound interest on ₹32,000 for 1½ years at 20% per annum, compounded half-yearly?

solution.concept: Half-yearly compounding: halve the rate and double the number of periods
solution.explanation: Rate per half-year = 10% and there are 3 half-years. Amount = 32,000 × 1.1³ = 32,000 × 1.331 = ₹42,592, so CI = ₹10,592.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9,600 is simple interest; ₹10,240 compounds annually for 1 year and then adds simple interest for the half-year.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum invested at compound interest (compounded annually) amounts to ₹13,310 in 3 years and to ₹14,641 in 4 years. What is the sum?

solution.concept: Consecutive annual amounts differ by one year's interest on the previous amount
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹11,000 discounts only 2 years; ₹9,317 subtracts 1,331 three times as if the interest were simple.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A loan taken at 10% per annum compound interest (compounded annually) is repaid in three equal annual instalments of ₹13,310 each, the first paid one year after the loan. What was the amount of the loan?

solution.concept: Loan = sum of the present values of the instalments
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹39,930 is the total repaid; ₹36,300 discounts all three instalments by one year only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹930. What is the compound interest on the same sum for 2 years at the same rate?

solution.concept: For 3 years, CI − SI = P(r/100)²(3 + r/100)
steps: 3-year CI = 33.1% of P; 3-year SI = 30% of P
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,000 is the 2-year simple interest; ₹9,930 is the 3-year compound interest; ₹6,600 takes 22% for two years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C start a business with ₹45,000, ₹60,000 and ₹75,000 respectively for one year. Out of a profit of ₹36,000, what is B's share?

solution.concept: Equal time: profit is shared in the ratio of capitals
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9,000 and ₹15,000 are A's and C's shares.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Neha starts a business with ₹30,000. After 4 months Vikram joins with ₹40,000. Three months after Vikram joins, Neha withdraws ₹10,000. Out of a profit of ₹63,000 at the end of the year, what is Vikram's share?

solution.explanation: Neha: 30,000 for 7 months and 20,000 for 5 months = 3,10,000. Vikram: 40,000 for 8 months = 3,20,000. Ratio 31 : 32, so Vikram gets 32/63 × 63,000 = ₹32,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹31,000 is Neha's share; ₹36,000 ignores time and uses the capital ratio 3 : 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Asha and Bina invest in a firm in the ratio 2 : 3. Asha manages the firm and takes 10% of the profit as salary; the remaining profit is shared in the ratio of investment. If Asha receives ₹27,600 in all, what is the total profit?

solution.concept: Working partner: salary first, then the balance in the capital ratio
solution.explanation: Asha gets 10% + 2/5 of 90% = 10% + 36% = 46% of the profit. 0.46 × profit = 27,600, so the profit is ₹60,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹69,000 ignores the salary and treats ₹27,600 as 2/5 of the profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: P and Q start a business with ₹24,000 and ₹36,000. After 6 months P adds ₹12,000 and Q withdraws ₹6,000. Three months later R joins with ₹45,000. If the profit at the end of the year is ₹79,200, what is R's share?

solution.concept: Month-weighted capital with changes during the year
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹32,000 and ₹35,200 are P's and Q's shares; ₹26,400 splits the profit equally.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In what ratio must rice costing ₹42 per kg be mixed with rice costing ₹54 per kg so that the mixture costs ₹46 per kg?

solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 writes the alligation differences the wrong way round.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 40-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio 3 : 2?

solution.concept: Milk stays constant when only water is added
solution.explanation: Milk = 30 L and water = 10 L. For 3 : 2 with 30 L of milk, water must be 20 L, so 10 L must be added.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 litres is the final quantity of water, not the amount to add.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A container holds 80 litres of pure milk. 8 litres are taken out and replaced with water. This is done two more times. How much milk is left in the container?

solution.concept: Repeated replacement: milk left = initial × (1 − x/V)ⁿ
solution.explanation: Each operation keeps 72/80 = 0.9 of the milk. After three operations, milk = 80 × 0.9³ = 80 × 0.729 = 58.32 L.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56 litres subtracts 8 litres of pure milk each time, ignoring that later withdrawals already contain water.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A merchant mixes tea costing ₹180 per kg with tea costing ₹240 per kg and sells the blend at ₹247.50 per kg, making a 25% profit. In what ratio did he mix the two teas?

solution.concept: Find the cost price of the mixture from the selling price, then apply alligation
solution.why_others_wrong: Using ₹247.50 directly as the mean gives no valid alligation (it lies above both prices); 3 : 7 reverses the ratio.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 60-litre vessel holds milk and water in the ratio 7 : 3. 20 litres of the mixture are drawn off and replaced with water. Then 20 litres of the new mixture are drawn off and replaced with pure milk. What is the final ratio of milk to water?

solution.concept: Each withdrawal removes the same fraction of both components
solution.explanation: Start: milk 42, water 18. Removing 20 L (one-third) leaves 28 and 12; adding water gives 28 : 32. Removing one-third again leaves 56/3 and 64/3; adding 20 L milk gives 116/3 : 64/3 = 29 : 16.
steps: Draw 20 L (1/3): milk 28, water 12; add 20 L water ⇒ 28 : 32
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 8 is the ratio after the first step only; 16 : 29 is reversed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Alloy A contains gold and copper in the ratio 5 : 3 and alloy B contains them in the ratio 2 : 3. How many kg of alloy B must be melted with 24 kg of alloy A to obtain an alloy with gold and copper in the ratio 3 : 2?

solution.concept: Alligation on the fraction of gold in each alloy
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 kg uses the ratio the wrong way round (24 ÷ 3); 6 kg compares the copper ratios incorrectly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can complete a piece of work in 12 days and B in 18 days. In how many days can they finish it working together?

solution.concept: Combined rate = sum of individual rates
solution.explanation: Take the work as 36 units (LCM of 12 and 18). A does 3 units a day and B 2, so together 5 units a day: 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 days averages the two times; 30 days adds them.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ramesh can paint a hall in 10 days and Suresh in 15 days. They paint it together and are paid ₹4,500. What is Ramesh's share?

solution.concept: Wages are shared in the ratio of work done, i.e. of efficiencies when they work for the same time
solution.explanation: Efficiencies are 1/10 : 1/15 = 3 : 2. Ramesh gets 3/5 × 4,500 = ₹2,700.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,800 shares in the ratio of days (10 : 15), which is the inverse of efficiency.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. They work on alternate days, A starting on the first day. On which day will the job be completed?

solution.concept: Work in 2-day cycles, then finish the remainder day by day
solution.explanation: Take the job as 60 units: A does 3 units a day and B 2. Each 2-day cycle does 5 units, so 11 cycles (22 days) do 55 units. On day 23, A does 3 more (58), and on day 24 B does the last 2 units.
steps: Day 24 (B): 60 units, so the job finishes on day 24
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 days is the time if both worked together every day; 23rd day forgets that A's 3 units on day 23 do not finish the job.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 8 men or 12 women can complete a project in 18 days. In how many days will 4 men and 12 women complete it together?

solution.concept: Convert everyone into one kind of worker
solution.explanation: 8 men = 12 women, so 1 man = 1.5 women. 4 men + 12 women = 6 + 12 = 18 women. The work is 12 × 18 = 216 woman-days, so 18 women take 216 ÷ 18 = 12 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 days treats 4 men + 12 women as twice the original team; 13.5 days converts women into men the wrong way.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B can complete a work in 24 days, B and C in 30 days, and C and A in 40 days. All three work together for 10 days, after which A leaves. B and C finish the remaining work. How many days does the whole work take?

solution.concept: Adding the three pair-rates gives twice the combined rate
solution.explanation: Take the work as 120 units: A + B = 5, B + C = 4, C + A = 3 units per day. So A + B + C = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 units a day. In 10 days they do 60 units; B and C finish the other 60 at 4 units a day in 15 days. Total = 25 days.
steps: Remaining 60 units at B + C = 4 units/day ⇒ 15 days
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 days is only the time B and C take after A leaves; 20 days is the time all three would take together.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 16 days and B in 24 days. With the help of C, the three finish it in 6 days and are paid ₹9,600 in total. What is C's share of the payment?

solution.concept: Find C's rate from the combined rate; wages follow the work done
solution.explanation: In 6 days A does 6/16 = 3/8 of the work and B does 6/24 = 1/4. C does the rest: 1 − 3/8 − 1/4 = 3/8. C's share = 3/8 × 9,600 = ₹3,600.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,200 splits equally; ₹2,400 is B's share; ₹4,800 gives C half the work.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours and pipe B can empty the full tank in 18 hours. If both are opened together when the tank is empty, in how many hours will it be full?

solution.concept: Net rate = filling rate − emptying rate
solution.explanation: Take the tank as 36 units: A fills 3 units an hour and B empties 2, a net of 1 unit an hour. The tank fills in 36 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.2 hours adds the two rates as if both pipes were filling.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 20 minutes and 30 minutes, while pipe C can empty it in 15 minutes. All three are opened on an empty tank, and after 10 minutes pipe C is closed. How many more minutes will it take to fill the tank?

solution.concept: Work in units; switch rates when a pipe is closed
solution.explanation: Take the tank as 60 units: A = 3, B = 2 and C = −4 units a minute. With all three open the tank gains 1 unit a minute, so 10 units in 10 minutes. The remaining 50 units at 5 units a minute take 10 more minutes.
steps: Capacity = 60 units; A = 3, B = 2, C = −4 per minute
All open: net 1 unit/min × 10 min = 10 units
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 minutes is the time A and B need for an empty tank; it ignores the 10 units already filled.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A pipe can fill a tank in 6 hours. Because of a leak at the bottom, it takes 7½ hours to fill the tank. In how many hours can the leak empty the full tank?

solution.concept: Leak rate = rate without leak − rate with leak
solution.explanation: Take the tank as 30 units. The pipe fills 5 units an hour; with the leak only 30 ÷ 7.5 = 4 units an hour. So the leak removes 1 unit an hour and empties the tank in 30 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 hours is just the delay (7.5 − 6); 13.5 hours adds the two times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A leak can empty a full tank in 6 hours. An inlet pipe that fills water at 4 litres per minute is opened at the moment the tank is full, and the tank now empties in 8 hours. What is the capacity of the tank?

solution.concept: Equate the net outflow rates and convert hours to minutes
solution.explanation: Let the capacity be C litres. The leak drains C/360 litres a minute. With the inlet, the net drain is C/480 a minute, so C/360 − 4 = C/480. This gives C/1440 = 4, so C = 5,760 litres.
steps: Net rate with inlet = C ÷ 480 L/min
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,440 and 1,920 litres are 4 L/min × 6 h and × 8 h, which is only what the inlet supplies in that time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A courier van goes from a bank's head office to a branch at 60 km/h and returns along the same road at 40 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole trip?

solution.concept: Average speed for equal distances = 2xy ÷ (x + y)
solution.explanation: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. For equal distances this is 2 × 60 × 40 ÷ (60 + 40) = 4,800 ÷ 100 = 48 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 km/h is the simple average of the two speeds, which is wrong because more time is spent at the slower speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two cars start at the same time from two towns 360 km apart and drive towards each other at 50 km/h and 70 km/h. After how long will they meet?

solution.concept: Objects moving towards each other: relative speed = sum of speeds
solution.explanation: They close the gap at 50 + 70 = 120 km/h, so they meet after 360 ÷ 120 = 3 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 hours uses the difference of the speeds (for the same direction); 7.2 hours uses only one car's speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A thief runs away at 9 km/h. A guard starts chasing him 15 minutes later at 12 km/h along the same road. How far will the guard have run when he catches the thief?

solution.concept: Chasing: time to catch = lead ÷ relative speed
solution.explanation: In 15 minutes the thief gets 9 × ¼ = 2.25 km ahead. The guard gains 12 − 9 = 3 km/h, so he takes 2.25 ÷ 3 = ¾ hour and runs 12 × ¾ = 9 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.75 km is the distance the thief runs during the chase; 2.25 km is only his lead.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cyclist covers the first third of a route at 30 km/h, the second third at 40 km/h and the last third at 60 km/h. What is the average speed for the whole route?

solution.concept: For equal distances, average speed is the harmonic mean of the speeds
solution.explanation: Take each third as 120 km (LCM of 30, 40, 60). Times: 4 h, 3 h and 2 h, total 9 h for 360 km, so the average is 40 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 43⅓ km/h is the simple average (30 + 40 + 60)/3, which applies only to equal times, not equal distances.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two trucks start at the same time from cities P and Q towards each other. After they meet, the first truck takes 9 hours to reach Q and the second takes 16 hours to reach P. If the first truck's speed is 36 km/h, what is the speed of the second truck?

steps: Let them meet after t hours: S₁t = 16S₂ and S₂t = 9S₁
solution.why_others_wrong: 20.25 km/h uses the ratio 16 : 9 without the square root; 48 km/h inverts the ratio.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Town X and town Y are 340 km apart. Bus A leaves X at 8:00 AM towards Y at 40 km/h. Bus B leaves Y at 9:00 AM towards X at 60 km/h. At what time do the two buses meet?

solution.concept: Head start, then relative speed of approach
solution.explanation: By 9:00 AM bus A has covered 40 km, leaving 300 km. The buses then close the gap at 40 + 60 = 100 km/h, taking 3 hours. They meet at 12:00 noon, 160 km from X.
steps: 8 to 9 AM: A covers 40 km; gap = 340 − 40 = 300 km
Check: A covers 40 × 4 = 160 km, B covers 60 × 3 = 180 km; total 340 km
solution.why_others_wrong: 11:24 AM assumes both buses started at 8:00 AM (340 ÷ 100 = 3.4 h).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's speed in still water is 15 km/h and the stream flows at 3 km/h. How long will the boat take to go 36 km downstream and come back?

solution.concept: Downstream speed = boat + stream; upstream speed = boat − stream
solution.explanation: Downstream speed = 18 km/h, so 36 km takes 2 hours. Upstream speed = 12 km/h, so 36 km takes 3 hours. Total = 5 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.8 hours ignores the stream (72 ÷ 15).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A motor boat covers 48 km upstream in 6 hours and 72 km downstream in 4 hours. What is the speed of the stream?

solution.explanation: Upstream speed = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 km/h and downstream speed = 72 ÷ 4 = 18 km/h. Stream = (18 − 8) ÷ 2 = 5 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 km/h is the boat's speed in still water; 10 km/h forgets to halve the difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat with a speed of 15 km/h in still water takes 3 hours longer to cover 60 km upstream than to cover 60 km downstream. How long will it take to go 60 km upstream and return?

solution.concept: Form an equation in the stream speed, then compute both legs
solution.explanation: 60/(15 − s) − 60/(15 + s) = 3 gives 120s = 3(225 − s²), i.e. s² + 40s − 225 = 0, so s = 5 km/h. Upstream speed 10 km/h (6 h), downstream 20 km/h (3 h): 9 hours in all.
solution.shortcut: Try the options' implied speeds: s = 5 gives 6 h and 3 h, a gap of exactly 3 h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 hours ignores the stream (120 ÷ 15); 6 hours is only the upstream leg.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train 240 m long runs at 54 km/h. How long will it take to cross a platform 210 m long?

solution.concept: Crossing a platform: distance = train length + platform length
solution.explanation: 54 km/h = 15 m/s. The train must cover 240 + 210 = 450 m, which takes 450 ÷ 15 = 30 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 seconds counts only the train's length; 14 seconds counts only the platform.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two trains 180 m and 220 m long run on parallel tracks in opposite directions at 50 km/h and 40 km/h. How long will they take to cross each other completely?

solution.concept: Opposite directions: add the speeds; distance = sum of lengths
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. The distance is 180 + 220 = 400 m, so the time is 400 ÷ 25 = 16 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 144 seconds subtracts the speeds (same direction); 8 seconds uses 200 m instead of the sum of the lengths; 20 seconds uses only the 50 km/h train's speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train crosses a signal pole in 12 seconds and a 300 m platform in 27 seconds. How long will it take to cross another train 360 m long coming from the opposite direction at 36 km/h?

solution.concept: Find the train's length and speed from two crossings, then use relative speed
solution.explanation: The extra 300 m takes 27 − 12 = 15 s, so the speed is 20 m/s and the length is 20 × 12 = 240 m. The other train moves at 36 km/h = 10 m/s towards it, so the relative speed is 30 m/s. Time = (240 + 360) ÷ 30 = 20 s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 seconds subtracts the speeds (same direction); 30 seconds ignores the other train's speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The perimeter of a rectangular plot is 76 m and its length is 24 m. What is its area?

solution.why_others_wrong: 456 m² takes the breadth as 76 ÷ 4 (a square); 624 m² forgets to halve the perimeter correctly, taking b = (76 − 24) ÷ 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A closed wooden box measures 12 cm × 8 cm × 5 cm. What is its total surface area?

solution.concept: Total surface area of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl)
solution.why_others_wrong: 480 is the volume (in cm³); 196 forgets the factor 2; 200 is the area of the four side faces only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A closed cylindrical water tank has a radius of 7 m and a height of 20 m. What is its total surface area? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: TSA of a closed cylinder = 2πr(r + h)
solution.why_others_wrong: 880 m² is the curved surface only; 1,034 m² adds only one circular end; 3,080 is the volume.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A circular garden has a radius of 14 m. A path 3.5 m wide runs around it on the outside. What is the area of the path? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Area of a ring = π(R² − r²)
solution.why_others_wrong: 308 m² multiplies the inner circumference by the width; 385 m² uses the outer circumference instead.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into small solid cones, each of base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. How many cones are made?

solution.concept: Volume is conserved when a solid is melted and recast
solution.explanation: Sphere volume = 4/3 π × 216 = 288π. Cone volume = 1/3 π × 9 × 4 = 12π. Number of cones = 288π ÷ 12π = 24.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 forgets the 1/3 in the cone's volume; 18 forgets the 4/3 in the sphere's volume.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Water flows through a cylindrical pipe of internal diameter 14 cm at 15 km/h into a rectangular tank 50 m long and 44 m wide. How long will it take for the water level in the tank to rise by 21 cm? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Volume delivered per hour = cross-section area × length of water column per hour
solution.explanation: Pipe radius = 7 cm = 0.07 m. Each hour a 15,000 m column flows in: 22/7 × 0.07² × 15,000 = 231 m³. The tank needs 50 × 44 × 0.21 = 462 m³, so the time is 462 ÷ 231 = 2 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 minutes uses 14 cm as the radius instead of the diameter (four times the area).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled together. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers is 8?

solution.concept: Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes (36 for two dice)
solution.explanation: The favourable outcomes are (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3) and (6, 2): 5 of 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/6 (= 6/36) is the probability of a sum of 7; 1/9 counts only 4 outcomes, missing one ordered pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is not blue?

solution.why_others_wrong: 1/3 is the probability of blue; 5/12 counts only red balls.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two cards are drawn together at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that one is a heart and the other is a spade?

solution.concept: Selections without replacement: count with combinations
solution.explanation: Ways to pick one heart and one spade = 13 × 13 = 169. Ways to pick any 2 cards = ⁵²C₂ = 1,326. P = 169/1,326 = 13/102.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/16 and 1/8 treat the draws as with replacement; 13/204 counts only the order 'heart first, then spade' within an unordered total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A box has 6 red and 4 white tokens. Three tokens are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that exactly two of them are red?

solution.concept: Hypergeometric selection: choose the reds and the whites separately
solution.explanation: Ways = ⁶C₂ × ⁴C₁ = 15 × 4 = 60. Total = ¹⁰C₃ = 120. P = 60/120 = 1/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 54/125 treats the draws as with replacement (3 × 0.6² × 0.4); 1/6 counts only one order, red-red-white (6/10 × 5/9 × 4/8); 1/8 forgets the factor ⁴C₁ = 4 for the white token (15/120).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers is a prime number or the product of the numbers is a multiple of 6?

solution.concept: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
solution.explanation: Sum prime: 15 outcomes. Product a multiple of 6: 15 outcomes. Both: 8 outcomes. So the union has 15 + 15 − 8 = 22 outcomes and P = 22/36 = 11/18.
steps: Product multiple of 6: 20 outcomes contain a 3 or 6; remove the 5 with both numbers odd ⇒ 15
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/6 adds the two counts without subtracting the 8 common outcomes; 5/12 counts only one event; 2/9 counts only the overlap.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Bag X contains 3 red and 5 black balls; bag Y contains 4 red and 4 black balls. One ball is drawn at random from X and put into Y without looking at it. Then a ball is drawn from Y. What is the probability that this ball is red?

solution.concept: Total probability: split on the colour of the transferred ball
solution.explanation: If a red ball is moved (probability 3/8), Y has 5 red of 9; if a black ball is moved (5/8), Y has 4 red of 9. P = 3/8 × 5/9 + 5/8 × 4/9 = 15/72 + 20/72 = 35/72.
steps: Red transferred: P = 3/8; then P(red from Y) = 5/9
Black transferred: P = 5/8; then P(red from Y) = 4/9
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 ignores the transfer; 7/16 averages the two bags' red proportions; 37/72 swaps 5/9 and 4/9 between the two cases.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A committee of 4 is to be formed from 6 men and 5 women so that it has exactly 2 men and 2 women. In how many ways can this be done?

solution.explanation: Choose 2 men in ⁶C₂ = 15 ways and 2 women in ⁵C₂ = 10 ways. Total = 15 × 10 = 150.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 adds the two counts instead of multiplying; 330 = ¹¹C₄ ignores the 2-and-2 condition; 300 counts ordered pairs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can the letters of the word BANKER be arranged so that the vowels always come together?

solution.concept: Treat the vowels as one block, then arrange inside the block
solution.explanation: The vowels A and E form one block. With B, N, K, R this gives 5 units: 5! = 120 arrangements. The vowels can be ordered inside the block in 2! = 2 ways. Total = 240.
steps: Letters: B, A, N, K, E, R (all different); vowels A, E
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 forgets the 2 internal orders (AE and EA); 720 is the number of arrangements with no restriction.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 4 boys and 3 girls sit in a row of 7 chairs so that no two girls sit next to each other?

solution.concept: Gap method: seat the unrestricted people first, then place the others in the gaps
solution.explanation: Seat the 4 boys in 4! = 24 ways. They create 5 gaps (including both ends). Place the 3 girls in 3 different gaps in ⁵P₃ = 60 ways. Total = 24 × 60 = 1,440.
steps: Girls in 3 of the 5 gaps, in order: ⁵P₃ = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60
solution.why_others_wrong: 240 uses ⁵C₃ and forgets that the girls are different people who can swap seats; 720 is 6!, from treating the girls as one block.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the total amount of car loans disbursed by all five branches together?

solution.explanation: Add the Car column: 45 + 60 + 35 + 70 + 40 = 250, i.e. ₹250 crore.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Education loans at the Patna branch form what percentage of all loans disbursed by the Patna branch?

solution.concept: Part ÷ whole × 100, with the branch total as the whole
solution.explanation: Patna's total = 90 + 35 + 40 + 35 = 200. Education loans = 40, so the share is 40 ÷ 200 × 100 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% divides by the other three loan types only (160); 16% divides by the wrong row total (Nagpur's 250).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the personal loans disbursed by Nagpur and Indore together to the education loans disbursed by Patna and Kochi together?

solution.explanation: Personal loans of Nagpur and Indore = 55 + 65 = 120. Education loans of Patna and Kochi = 40 + 45 = 85. 120 : 85 = 24 : 17.
solution.why_others_wrong: 17 : 24 is the ratio reversed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage is the average home loan disbursed per branch more than the average car loan disbursed per branch?

solution.concept: Percentage more = difference ÷ base × 100, with the car-loan average as the base
solution.explanation: Average home loan = 650 ÷ 5 = 130 and average car loan = 250 ÷ 5 = 50. The excess is 80, which is 160% of 50.
solution.shortcut: Averages over the same 5 branches compare like totals: (650 − 250) ÷ 250 = 160%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 61.54% uses the home-loan average as the base; 260% is the ratio 130 ÷ 50 expressed as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2026-27, Kochi's home loans grow by 20% and its car loans fall by 10% over 2025-26, while its other loans stay the same. Kochi's total loans in 2026-27 will be what percentage of the combined 2025-26 loans of Patna and Surat?

solution.concept: Apply each change to its own category, then compare totals
solution.why_others_wrong: 87.5% uses Kochi's unchanged total (350); 96.5% applies the home-loan rise but forgets the fall in car loans.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many men are employed in company R?

solution.why_others_wrong: 540 is the number of women; 720 uses 60% for men.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The number of women in tech roles in company S is what percent more than that in company Q?

solution.concept: Two-level percentages, then 'percent more than' on the right base
solution.explanation: Women in tech: S = 50% of (32% of 2,500) = 400; Q = 30% of (40% of 2,000) = 240. S has 160 more, which is 160/240 = 66⅔% more than Q.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% uses S (400) as the base; 20% subtracts the percentages 50 − 30; 166⅔% is 400 as a percentage of 240.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the number of women not in tech roles in company P to that in company Q?

solution.concept: Complement percentages applied to the number of women
solution.explanation: P: women = 560, 75% not in tech = 420. Q: women = 800, 70% not in tech = 560. 420 : 560 = 3 : 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 10 is the ratio of all women (560 : 800); 7 : 8 applies Q's women percentage (40%) instead of its non-tech share (70%), giving 420 : 480; 4 : 3 is reversed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average number of women working in non-tech roles across the five companies?

solution.concept: Average of derived values computed per company
solution.explanation: Women not in tech: P 420, Q 560, R 432, S 400, T 270. Total = 2,082, so the average is 2,082 ÷ 5 = 416.4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 630 is the average number of all women; 213.6 is the average number of women in tech roles.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 20% of the men in company T also work in tech roles, what percentage of company T's tech-role employees are women?

solution.concept: Build the tech-role group from both genders before taking the share
solution.explanation: T has 450 women, 180 of them in tech. Men = 1,800 − 450 = 1,350, and 20% of them = 270 are in tech. Tech employees = 180 + 270 = 450, of whom women are 180/450 = 40%.
steps: Women in T = 25% of 1,800 = 450; in tech = 40% of 450 = 180
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% is the share of women among all employees of T; 13⅓% divides 180 by all men; 60% is the men's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average number of two-wheelers sold per month over the six months?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sales in April were what percent less than the sales in March?

solution.concept: Percent less than = difference ÷ the larger (reference) value × 100
solution.explanation: March = 600 and April = 380. The fall of 220 is 220/600 = 36⅔% of March's sales.
solution.why_others_wrong: 57.89% divides by April's sales; 63⅓% is April as a percentage of March.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the combined sales of January, March and May to the combined sales of February, April and June?

solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 8 is reversed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many of the six months were the sales strictly more than the six-month average?

solution.concept: Compare each month with the average
solution.explanation: The average is 500. Sales above 500 were in February (520), March (600) and May (550): 3 months. June (500) equals the average and does not count.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 counts June, whose sales equal the average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which year did branch X record the highest percentage increase in deposits over the previous year?

solution.concept: Percentage change = change ÷ previous year's value
solution.why_others_wrong: 2022 and 2025 have the same absolute rise of 60, but on larger or smaller bases; 2022's 25% is still below 2024's 28.57%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The total deposits mobilised by branch Y over the five years are what percentage of the total deposits mobilised by branch X over the same period?

solution.concept: Ratio of totals as a percentage
solution.why_others_wrong: 109.59% is X as a percentage of Y; 8.75% is the gap (140) as a percentage of X.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The combined deposits of both branches in 2024 and 2025 together are what percent more than their combined deposits in 2021 and 2022 together?

solution.concept: Sum four bars on each side, then compute the percentage increase on the earlier total
solution.why_others_wrong: 31.51% divides by the later total (1,460); 146% is the later total as a percentage of the earlier one.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much does the family spend on food each month?

solution.explanation: Food has 72°, which is 72/360 = 1/5 of the income. 1/5 × 72,000 = ₹14,400.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹18,000 is the rent (90°); ₹7,200 is transport (36°).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the monthly income does the family save?

solution.explanation: Savings = 63°, so the share is 63 ÷ 360 × 100 = 17.5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 63% reads the angle as a percentage; 12.6% divides by 500 instead of 360.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The family's spending on rent is what percent more than its spending on education?

solution.concept: Percentages can be compared directly from the angles
solution.explanation: Rent = 90° and education = 54°. The excess is 36°, which is 36/54 = 66⅔% of education.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40% uses rent as the base (36/90); 36% reads the angle difference as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how many rupees does the family's spending on rent and transport together exceed its spending on education and others together?

solution.concept: Work with angles first, convert to rupees once
solution.explanation: Rent + transport = 90° + 36° = 126°. Education + others = 54° + 45° = 99°. The gap of 27° is 27/360 × 72,000 = ₹5,400.
solution.shortcut: Each degree is ₹200, so the answer is just 27 × 200.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,400 leaves out 'Others' (126° − 54° = 72°); ₹16,200 leaves out education (126° − 45° = 81°); ₹2,700 takes 1° as ₹100.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the number of boys in Science to the number of girls in Arts?

solution.concept: Boys in a stream = students in the stream − girls in the stream
solution.explanation: Science students = 25% of 3,600 = 900; Science girls = 20% of 1,500 = 300; so Science boys = 600. Arts girls = 32% of 1,500 = 480. 600 : 480 = 5 : 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 : 5 is reversed; 25 : 32 compares the two percentages, which are of different totals.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The number of girls in Science and Law together is what percentage of the number of boys in Arts and Law together?

solution.concept: Derive boys stream-wise from the two charts, then take the percentage
steps: Girls in Science = 300; in Law = 8% of 1,500 = 120 ⇒ 420
solution.why_others_wrong: 114.29% is the inverse (480 ÷ 420); 46.67% uses all Arts and Law students (900) as the base.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 25% of the girls and 40% of the boys in the Management stream got campus placements, what percentage of all Management students got placed?

solution.concept: Weighted percentage over girls and boys of one stream
solution.explanation: Management has 540 students, of whom 180 are girls and 360 boys. Placed = 25% of 180 + 40% of 360 = 45 + 144 = 189, which is 189/540 = 35%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32.5% is the simple average of 25% and 40%, ignoring that there are twice as many boys as girls.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the profit increase from 2022 to 2023?

solution.explanation: Profit rose from 56 to 70, an increase of 14. 14 ÷ 56 × 100 = 25%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% uses 2023 as the base (14 ÷ 70); 14% reads the increase in lakh as a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average annual profit of the company over the seven years?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹60 lakh averages only the first and last years ((40 + 80) ÷ 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2023 the company's expenses were ₹280 lakh, and profit = income − expenses. What was the profit as a percentage of income in 2023?

solution.concept: Income = expenses + profit; margin on income
solution.explanation: Income = 280 + 70 = ₹350 lakh. Profit as a percentage of income = 70 ÷ 350 × 100 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% divides the profit by the expenses instead of the income; 80% is the expenses' share of income.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which year was the percentage change in profit over the previous year the largest (ignoring whether it was a rise or a fall)?

solution.concept: Compare percentage changes, not absolute changes
solution.why_others_wrong: 2025 has the largest absolute rise (17 lakh), but on a bigger base; 2022 and 2023 have the same rise of 14, and 2022's base is smaller.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the units manufactured in 2023 were sold in 2023?

solution.explanation: In 2023, 75 thousand units were made and 60 thousand sold. 60 ÷ 75 × 100 = 80%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 125% inverts the ratio; 20% is the unsold share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Over the five years, the total number of unsold units is what percentage of the total number of units manufactured?

solution.concept: Gap between two lines, summed over the period
solution.explanation: Total manufactured = 360 thousand and total sold = 315 thousand, so 45 thousand were unsold. 45 ÷ 360 × 100 = 12.5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14.29% divides by the units sold (315); 87.5% is the sold share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Each unit sells at ₹2,500. In 2024 the company also cleared all the units left unsold in 2023 at a 20% discount. What was its total revenue in 2024 from these two sources?

solution.concept: Revenue = units × price; the unsold units of a year are the gap between the two lines
solution.explanation: Regular sales in 2024 = 72,000 × 2,500 = ₹18 crore. Unsold in 2023 = 75,000 − 60,000 = 15,000 units, cleared at ₹2,000 each = ₹3 crore. Total = ₹21 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹21.75 crore ignores the 20% discount; ₹18 crore leaves out the clearance sale.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many customers of the branch hold all three products?

solution.concept: The 'remaining' group is 100% minus all the listed groups
solution.explanation: The listed groups add up to 40 + 15 + 10 + 12 + 8 + 5 = 90%, so 10% hold all three: 10% of 1,200 = 120.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many customers hold a fixed deposit?

solution.concept: Every region of the Venn diagram that includes FD
solution.explanation: FD holders = only FD (180) + savings and FD (144) + FD and card (60) + all three (120) = 504.
solution.why_others_wrong: 180 counts only those with FD alone; 384 leaves out those with all three products.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many customers hold exactly two of the three products?

solution.concept: 'Exactly two' excludes those holding all three
solution.why_others_wrong: 420 also counts the 120 customers with all three products.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the number of customers holding a savings account to the number holding a credit card?

solution.concept: Total holders of a product = sum of every region containing it
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 : 1 compares only the single-product groups (480 : 120); 33 : 70 is reversed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next month, 25% of the customers who hold only a savings account also open an FD, and nothing else changes. What percentage of the branch's customers will then hold exactly two products?

solution.concept: Track which Venn region the moving customers leave and join
solution.explanation: 25% of the 480 savings-only customers = 120 customers move from 'only savings' to 'savings and FD'. Exactly two becomes 300 + 120 = 420, which is 35% of 1,200.
steps: They now hold savings + FD only (exactly two)
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% ignores the movers; 45% also includes the customers who hold all three.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many packages for Himachal did the agency sell?

solution.concept: Remainder share within the domestic group
solution.explanation: Domestic packages = 60% of 1,500 = 900. Himachal gets 100 − 35 − 25 = 40% of them: 360.
solution.why_others_wrong: 315 is the Goa figure; 540 takes 60% of 900.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the revenue from Singapore packages to the revenue from Dubai packages?

solution.concept: Revenue = number of packages × average price
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 5 compares the number of packages only; 5 : 4 compares the prices only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The number of Thailand packages sold was what percent less than the number of Kerala packages sold?

solution.explanation: Kerala = 25% of 900 = 225 and Thailand = 36% of 600 = 216. The gap of 9 is 9/225 = 4% of Kerala's figure.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4⅙% divides by Thailand's figure; 11% subtracts the two percentages (36 − 25), which are of different bases.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average revenue per domestic package?

solution.concept: Weighted average price = total revenue ÷ total packages
solution.explanation: Goa: 315 × 24,000 = ₹75.6 lakh; Kerala: 225 × 30,000 = ₹67.5 lakh; Himachal: 360 × 20,000 = ₹72 lakh. Total = ₹2,15,10,000 for 900 packages, i.e. ₹23,900 per package.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹24,666.67 is the simple average of the three prices and ignores how many packages were sold at each.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The agency earns a commission of 8% on domestic revenue and 5% on international revenue. What is its total commission for the quarter?

solution.concept: Apply each rate to its own revenue base
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹38,69,100 swaps the two rates; ₹17,46,000 is the international commission alone; ₹36,67,950 applies the average rate 6.5% to all revenue.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many items did store B sell?

solution.explanation: 90 items are 12% of the items sold, so items sold = 90 ÷ 0.12 = 750.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,080 multiplies 90 by 12; 660 is the number of items kept.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the items sold by store D were returned?

solution.explanation: Store D sold 64 + 736 = 800 items, so the return rate is 64 ÷ 800 × 100 = 8%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.7% divides by the items kept (736) instead of the items sold.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking all five stores together, what percentage of the items sold were returned?

solution.concept: Overall rate = total returned ÷ total sold, after filling every missing cell
solution.explanation: Fill the gaps: A returned 15% of 800 = 120; B sold 750; C returned 1,200 − 1,020 = 180; D sold 800; E returned 92 of 1,000. Total sold = 4,550 and total returned = 546, so the overall rate is 546 ÷ 4,550 = 12%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.84% averages the five stores' percentages without weighting by items sold; 13.64% divides by the items kept (4,004); 88% is the share kept.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the principal invested in scheme S2?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹33,600 is the amount (principal plus interest); ₹96,000 ignores the time of 4 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The interest earned in scheme S1 is what percentage of the interest earned in scheme S2?

solution.concept: Fill the missing interest first, then compare
solution.why_others_wrong: 160% is S2 as a percentage of S1; 37.5% is the gap as a percentage of S2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If the principal of scheme S3 were instead invested for 2 years at compound interest (compounded annually) at the same rate as S3, what interest would it earn?

solution.concept: Find the missing rate from the table, then apply compound interest
solution.shortcut: 2-year CI = 2 × 7% + 0.49% = 14.49% of the principal.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹5,600 is the 2-year simple interest; ₹45,796 is the amount, not the interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Simple interest on ₹8,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years
Quantity II: Compound interest on ₹8,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years, compounded annually

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: SI over 3 years vs CI over 2 years
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 8,000 × 10% × 3 = ₹2,400. Quantity II = 8,000 × 21% = ₹1,680. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' comes from assuming compound interest is always larger, without noticing the different periods.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The average of the first ten even natural numbers
Quantity II: √121 − 1

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Average of an arithmetic sequence = average of first and last terms
solution.explanation: The first ten even numbers are 2 to 20, with average (2 + 20) ÷ 2 = 11. Quantity II = 11 − 1 = 10. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: '= or cannot be established' comes from averaging 2 to 18 (only nine even numbers, average 10); 'Quantity I < Quantity II' comes from averaging the first ten natural numbers (5.5).
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The value of x, where x² − 14x + 48 = 0
Quantity II: 7

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A quantity with two possible values can lie on either side of a fixed number
solution.explanation: x² − 14x + 48 = (x − 6)(x − 8) = 0, so x = 6 or 8. 6 < 7 but 8 > 7, so no single relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' takes only the larger root.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The speed (km/h) of a boat in still water if it goes downstream at 22 km/h and upstream at 14 km/h
Quantity II: The speed (km/h) of a cyclist who covers 50 km in 2 hours 30 minutes

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Boat speed = (downstream + upstream) ÷ 2; speed = distance ÷ time
solution.explanation: Quantity I = (22 + 14) ÷ 2 = 18 km/h. Quantity II = 50 ÷ 2.5 = 20 km/h. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' uses the downstream speed 22 km/h as the boat's speed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Profit percentage when an article is marked 30% above its cost price and sold at a 10% discount
Quantity II: Profit percentage when the cost price of 20 articles equals the selling price of 17 articles

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Markup–discount profit vs 'cost of n = selling price of m' profit
solution.explanation: Quantity I: 1.3 × 0.9 = 1.17, so 17%. Quantity II: profit = (20 − 17) ÷ 17 = 3/17 ≈ 17.65%. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
steps: II: let CP of 1 article = 1; 17 articles sell for 20
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' comes from computing II as 3/20 = 15% (using 20 as the base instead of 17).
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of different arrangements of the letters of the word LEVEL
Quantity II: The number of ways of choosing 2 members from a group of 8

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Arrangements with repeated letters: n! ÷ (p! q!)
solution.explanation: LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice: 5! ÷ (2! × 2!) = 120 ÷ 4 = 30. ⁸C₂ = 28. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' comes from dividing 5! by 2! three times (120 ÷ 8 = 15) or from using ⁸P₂ = 56 for Quantity II; a selection of 2 members is unordered, so ⁸C₂ is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Days taken by A and B together, if A is 50% more efficient than B and B alone takes 30 days
Quantity II: Days taken by C alone, if C and D together take 9 days and D alone takes 18 days

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Efficiency and time are inversely proportional
solution.explanation: A is 1.5 times as efficient as B, so A alone takes 30 ÷ 1.5 = 20 days and A + B take 1 ÷ (1/20 + 1/30) = 12 days. C's rate = 1/9 − 1/18 = 1/18, so C takes 18 days. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' comes from subtracting days instead of rates for C (18 − 9 = 9 days).
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the speed of the train?
I. The train crosses a 200 m long platform in 18 seconds.
II. The train crosses a signal pole in 10 seconds.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Two unknowns (length and speed) need two independent equations
solution.explanation: Statement I gives L + 200 = 18v and statement II gives L = 10v; each has two unknowns. Together, 10v + 200 = 18v, so v = 25 m/s (90 km/h). Both statements are needed.
steps: I alone: L + 200 = 18v — L unknown, not sufficient
II alone: L = 10v — L unknown, not sufficient
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Statement I alone' is tempting because the platform length is known, but the train's own length is not.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the principal deposited by Kavya?
I. The simple interest on it for 3 years at 8% per annum is ₹4,800.
II. The compound interest on it for 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually, is ₹4,200.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not

solution.concept: Each statement fixes the rate and time, leaving only the principal unknown
solution.explanation: From I: P = 4,800 × 100 ÷ (8 × 3) = ₹20,000. From II: 0.21P = 4,200, so P = ₹20,000. Each statement alone answers the question.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Both together' is a common choice when one statement looks complicated (compound interest), but II alone has only one unknown.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is Rahul's present age?
I. Rahul is 4 years older than Sita.
II. The ratio of the present ages of Sita and Mohan is 3 : 4.
III. The average present age of Rahul, Sita and Mohan is 28 years.

options.text: Any two of the three statements are sufficient
Only statements I and III together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Three unknowns need three independent equations
solution.explanation: There are three unknown ages. I gives R = S + 4, II gives M = 4S/3 and III gives R + S + M = 84. Any two leave one unknown free; all three give S + 4 + S + 4S/3 = 84, so S = 24 and R = 28.
steps: I: R = S + 4; II: M = 4S/3; III: R + S + M = 84
Any two statements: 2 equations, 3 unknowns — not sufficient
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and III' looks enough because III ties all three ages, but without II Mohan's age is free (R + S + M = 84 with R = S + 4 has many solutions).
solution.final_answer: Option C: All three statements together are necessary

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: At what rate of interest per annum is a bank lending money?
I. A sum lent at this rate of simple interest doubles itself in 8 years.
II. The simple interest on ₹5,000 for 4 years at this rate is ₹2,500.
III. On ₹16,000 lent for 2 years at this rate, compound interest (compounded annually) exceeds simple interest by ₹250.

options.text: Any one of the three statements alone is sufficient
Either I alone or II alone is sufficient, but III alone is not
Only II and III together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary

solution.concept: Each statement is a single equation in the rate alone
solution.explanation: I: interest of 100% in 8 years gives R = 12.5%. II: 5,000 × R × 4 ÷ 100 = 2,500 gives R = 12.5%. III: for 2 years, CI − SI = P(R/100)², so 16,000 × (R/100)² = 250, (R/100)² = 1/64 and R = 12.5%. Each statement alone is sufficient.
solution.why_others_wrong: Many reject III alone, not recalling the 2-year formula CI − SI = P(R/100)²; the negative root is impossible for a rate, so III gives a unique answer.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Any one of the three statements alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits second to the right of Chetan?

solution.concept: Linear arrangement: all facing north, so right means further east
solution.explanation: With everyone facing north, the right of a person is towards seat 6. Chetan is at seat 3, so second to his right is seat 5: Farah.
steps: Divya cannot be at the left end (it pushes Farah to an end), so Divya = 6, Chetan = 3, Bina = 4
Anil and Farah must be three seats apart among seats 1, 2, 5: Anil = 2, Farah = 5; Eshan = 1
Left to right: Eshan, Anil, Chetan, Bina, Farah, Divya
Second to the right of Chetan (3) is seat 5: Farah
solution.why_others_wrong: Anil is immediately to Chetan's left (counting the wrong way); Bina is immediately to his right; Divya is third to his right.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons sit between Eshan and Farah?

solution.explanation: Eshan is at seat 1 and Farah at seat 5, so the persons in seats 2 to 4 (Anil, Chetan and Bina) sit between them: 3.
steps: Left to right: Eshan, Anil, Chetan, Bina, Farah, Divya

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits at the extreme left end of the row?

solution.explanation: Divya is forced to the right end, so the left end is the only seat left after placing everyone else: Eshan.
steps: Left to right: Eshan, Anil, Chetan, Bina, Farah, Divya
solution.why_others_wrong: Divya sits at the right end, not the left; Anil and Chetan are at seats 2 and 3.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true according to the arrangement?

options.text: Bina sits exactly in the middle of Chetan and Farah
Eshan sits immediately to the left of Chetan
Two persons sit between Anil and Divya
Farah sits at the extreme right end

solution.concept: Checking statements against the final arrangement
solution.explanation: Chetan (3), Bina (4) and Farah (5) sit in consecutive seats, so Bina is exactly in the middle of them.
steps: Left to right: Eshan, Anil, Chetan, Bina, Farah, Divya
Bina between Chetan (3) and Farah (5): true
Immediately left of Chetan (3) is Anil (2), not Eshan: false
The right end (6) is Divya: false
Between Anil (2) and Divya (6) sit three persons: false
solution.final_answer: Option A: Bina sits exactly in the middle of Chetan and Farah

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits second to the left of Jaya?

solution.concept: Mixed facing directions: left and right depend on the person's facing
solution.explanation: Jaya is at seat 5 facing south, so her left is towards the east. Second to her left is seat 7: Gaurav.
steps: Kunal must be at the west end (the east-end case puts Nidhi on Jaya's seat)
West to east: Kunal (S), Mohit (S), Nidhi (N), Hema (N), Jaya (S), Ishaan (N), Gaurav (S), Lata (N)
Jaya faces south, so her left is eastward: seat 5 + 2 = 7
solution.why_others_wrong: Nidhi is second to the west of Jaya, which would be her left only if she faced north; Ishaan is immediately to her left; Lata is third to her left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons face north?

solution.concept: Reading the facing directions from the solved row
solution.explanation: Nidhi, Hema, Ishaan and Lata face north; the other four face south. So 4 persons face north.
steps: West to east: Kunal (S), Mohit (S), Nidhi (N), Hema (N), Jaya (S), Ishaan (N), Gaurav (S), Lata (N)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the position of Gaurav with respect to Mohit?

solution.concept: Relative position for a south-facing person
solution.explanation: Mohit is at seat 2 facing south, so his left is towards the east. Gaurav is at seat 7, five seats east of Mohit: fifth to Mohit's left.
steps: West to east: Kunal (S), Mohit (S), Nidhi (N), Hema (N), Jaya (S), Ishaan (N), Gaurav (S), Lata (N)
Gaurav = seat 7, i.e. 5 seats to the east
So Gaurav is fifth to the left of Mohit
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fifth to the right' is what you get if you forget that Mohit faces south.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Fifth to the left

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of persons sit at the two extreme ends of the row?

solution.explanation: Seat 1 is Kunal and seat 8 is Lata.
steps: West to east: Kunal (S), Mohit (S), Nidhi (N), Hema (N), Jaya (S), Ishaan (N), Gaurav (S), Lata (N)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits third to the right of Nidhi?

solution.concept: Counting to the right of a north-facing person
solution.explanation: Nidhi is at seat 3 facing north, so her right is eastward: seat 3 + 3 = 6, which is Ishaan.
steps: West to east: Kunal (S), Mohit (S), Nidhi (N), Hema (N), Jaya (S), Ishaan (N), Gaurav (S), Lata (N)
Nidhi = 3 (north) → third to the right = seat 6 = Ishaan
solution.why_others_wrong: Jaya is second to Nidhi's right and Gaurav fourth; Mohit is on her left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who faces the person who sits second to the left of Zoya?

solution.concept: Double row: find the seat, then cross to the facing row
solution.explanation: Zoya sits at seat 4 of Row 2 facing north, so her left is towards the west. Second to her left is seat 2 of Row 2 (Oviya), who faces seat 2 of Row 1: Uday.
steps: Row membership: {Zoya, Yamini, Wasim} with Sahil and Oviya in Row 2; the rest in Row 1
Row 1 (facing south), west to east: Rekha, Uday, Tanvi, Vimal, Pranav; Row 2 (facing north), west to east: Wasim, Oviya, Sahil, Zoya, Yamini
Second to the left of Zoya (Row 2, seat 4, facing north) = Row 2 seat 2 = Oviya
The person facing Row 2 seat 2 is Row 1 seat 2 = Uday
solution.why_others_wrong: Vimal faces Zoya herself; Tanvi faces Sahil; Rekha faces Wasim.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which two persons sit at the extreme ends of the row that faces south?

solution.explanation: Row 1 faces south; its end seats are held by Rekha and Pranav.
steps: Row 1 (facing south), west to east: Rekha, Uday, Tanvi, Vimal, Pranav; Row 2 (facing north), west to east: Wasim, Oviya, Sahil, Zoya, Yamini
solution.why_others_wrong: Wasim and Yamini are the ends of the north-facing row.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons sit between Wasim and Yamini?

solution.explanation: Wasim and Yamini both sit in Row 2, at seats 1 and 5, so Oviya, Sahil and Zoya sit between them: 3.
steps: Row 1 (facing south), west to east: Rekha, Uday, Tanvi, Vimal, Pranav; Row 2 (facing north), west to east: Wasim, Oviya, Sahil, Zoya, Yamini

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true?

options.text: Oviya sits immediately to the right of Sahil
Rekha sits immediately to the left of Uday

solution.concept: Checking statements in a double-row arrangement
solution.explanation: Tanvi is at seat 3 of Row 1 and Sahil at seat 3 of Row 2, so they face each other.
steps: Row 1 (facing south), west to east: Rekha, Uday, Tanvi, Vimal, Pranav; Row 2 (facing north), west to east: Wasim, Oviya, Sahil, Zoya, Yamini
Tanvi (Row 1, seat 3) faces Sahil (Row 2, seat 3): true
Pranav (Row 1, seat 5) faces Yamini, not Zoya: false
Sahil faces north, so his right is seat 4 (Zoya), not Oviya: false
Uday faces south, so his left is east (seat 3, Tanvi), not Rekha: false

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits opposite Meera?

solution.explanation: In a six-seat circle the opposite seat is three places away. Three places from Meera is Priya.
steps: Going to the right (anticlockwise) from Kavya: Kavya, Meera, Omkar, Lalit, Priya, Naveen
solution.why_others_wrong: Lalit is opposite Kavya; Omkar is Meera's neighbour; Naveen is opposite Omkar.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits second to the left of Omkar?

solution.concept: Left of a centre-facing person is the clockwise direction
solution.explanation: Going left (clockwise) from Omkar: Meera, then Kavya.
steps: Going to the right (anticlockwise) from Kavya: Kavya, Meera, Omkar, Lalit, Priya, Naveen
Left of Omkar: Meera, then Kavya
solution.why_others_wrong: Priya is second to Omkar's right; Lalit and Meera are his immediate neighbours.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits immediately to the left of Kavya?

solution.explanation: Meera is on Kavya's right; the seat on her left belongs to Naveen.
steps: Going to the right (anticlockwise) from Kavya: Kavya, Meera, Omkar, Lalit, Priya, Naveen

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons sit between Omkar and Naveen when counted to the right of Omkar?

solution.concept: Counting in one direction around a circle
solution.explanation: Moving right from Omkar: Lalit, Priya, then Naveen. So 2 persons sit between them in that direction.
steps: Going to the right (anticlockwise) from Kavya: Kavya, Meera, Omkar, Lalit, Priya, Naveen
Right of Omkar: Lalit, Priya, Naveen

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits second to the left of Deepa?

solution.concept: Left of a centre-facing person is clockwise
solution.explanation: Deepa faces the centre, so her left is clockwise: Harsh, then Bhavna.
steps: Case (a) (Bhavna between Farhan and Harsh on Gita's side) fails on Isha's direction
Anticlockwise from Aarav: Aarav (centre), Gita (outside), Chirag (centre), Isha (centre), Farhan (outside), Bhavna (centre), Harsh (outside), Deepa (centre)
Deepa faces the centre; clockwise from her: Harsh, Bhavna
solution.why_others_wrong: Gita is second to Deepa's right; Aarav is immediately to her right; Farhan is third to her left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons sit between Gita and Harsh when counted to the right of Gita?

solution.concept: Counting to the right of an outside-facing person
solution.explanation: Gita faces outside, so her right is clockwise: Aarav, Deepa, then Harsh. Two persons sit between them.
steps: Anticlockwise from Aarav: Aarav (centre), Gita (outside), Chirag (centre), Isha (centre), Farhan (outside), Bhavna (centre), Harsh (outside), Deepa (centre)
Gita faces outside → her right is clockwise
Clockwise from Gita: Aarav, Deepa, Harsh

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following persons face outside?

solution.explanation: Exactly three persons face outside: Farhan, Gita and Harsh.
steps: Anticlockwise from Aarav: Aarav (centre), Gita (outside), Chirag (centre), Isha (centre), Farhan (outside), Bhavna (centre), Harsh (outside), Deepa (centre)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Farhan, Gita and Harsh

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the position of Isha with respect to Chirag?

solution.explanation: Chirag faces the centre, so his right is anticlockwise, and the next seat anticlockwise from Chirag is Isha's.
steps: Anticlockwise from Aarav: Aarav (centre), Gita (outside), Chirag (centre), Isha (centre), Farhan (outside), Bhavna (centre), Harsh (outside), Deepa (centre)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Immediately to the right

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits opposite Isha?

solution.concept: Opposite seats in an eight-seat circle
solution.explanation: Opposite means four seats away: Deepa.
steps: Anticlockwise from Aarav: Aarav (centre), Gita (outside), Chirag (centre), Isha (centre), Farhan (outside), Bhavna (centre), Harsh (outside), Deepa (centre)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits second to the right of the person from Kanpur?

solution.concept: Square table: side-seat persons face outside, so their right is clockwise
solution.explanation: Neel (Kanpur) sits at the middle of a side and faces outside, so his right is clockwise: Manju, then Komal.
steps: Sneha must be at a side seat with Rohan at the corner to her left

Anticlockwise from Jatin: Jatin (Indore, corner), Sneha (Agra, side), Rohan (Mysuru, corner), Komal (Jaipur, side), Manju (Bhopal, corner), Neel (Kanpur, side), Lokesh (Dehradun, corner), Pallavi (Cochin, side)
Neel faces outside: clockwise from Neel → Manju, Komal
solution.why_others_wrong: Pallavi is second to Neel's left; Lokesh is immediately to his left; Manju is immediately to his right.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: The person from which city sits immediately to the left of Manju?

solution.concept: Corner seats face the centre, so the left is clockwise
solution.explanation: Manju sits at a corner facing the centre; her immediate left is the clockwise seat, held by Komal, who is from Jaipur.
steps: Anticlockwise from Jatin: Jatin (Indore, corner), Sneha (Agra, side), Rohan (Mysuru, corner), Komal (Jaipur, side), Manju (Bhopal, corner), Neel (Kanpur, side), Lokesh (Dehradun, corner), Pallavi (Cochin, side)
