solution.why_others_wrong: Kanpur (Neel) is on Manju's right; Bhopal is Manju's own city; Mysuru is Rohan's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Seven trainees Pooja, Qasim, Rahul, Sana, Tejas, Urvi and Vinay attend one training session each on the seven days of a week from Monday to Sunday, one trainee per day. Each session is on a different subject among Audit, Credit, Forex, Insurance, Loans, Risk and Treasury.
- Exactly three sessions are held after Pooja's session.
- Urvi attends the Credit session on the day immediately after Pooja.
- Rahul attends on a day after Urvi, but not on Sunday.
- Tejas attends on a weekend day and his subject is Insurance.
- The Forex session is held on the day immediately before Sana's session.
- Only one session is held between the Audit session and the Credit session.
- The Treasury session is held on the day immediately after the Audit session.
- The Loans session is held after the Treasury session.
- Qasim attends the Risk session, on a day before Vinay's.

Who attends on Tuesday, and on which subject?

solution.explanation: Pooja = Thursday, Urvi (Credit) = Friday. Audit is two days from Credit: Wednesday (Sunday would leave no day after it for Treasury). Treasury = Thursday (Pooja). Rahul is after Friday but not on Sunday, so Rahul = Saturday and Tejas (Insurance) = Sunday; Loans, after Treasury, is Saturday (Rahul). Monday to Wednesday remain for Qasim, Sana and Vinay; Forex is the day before Sana and Qasim (Risk) is before Vinay. The only fit is Qasim (Risk) Monday, Vinay (Forex) Tuesday, Sana (Audit) Wednesday.
steps: Pooja = Thursday (three days after her); Urvi = Friday (Credit)
Audit = Wednesday (Sunday fails: Treasury must follow Audit); Treasury = Thursday
Rahul = Saturday (after Friday, not Sunday); Tejas = Sunday (Insurance); Loans = Saturday
Sana on Monday has no Forex day before her; Sana on Tuesday needs Forex on Monday (Vinay, since Qasim has Risk), but then Qasim would be on Wednesday, which is Audit: rejected
So Sana = Wednesday (Audit), Forex = Tuesday = Vinay, Qasim (Risk) = Monday
Final: Mon Qasim (Risk), Tue Vinay (Forex), Wed Sana (Audit), Thu Pooja (Treasury), Fri Urvi (Credit), Sat Rahul (Loans), Sun Tejas (Insurance)
solution.why_others_wrong: Sana attends Audit on Wednesday; Qasim's subject is Risk (Monday).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
All pens are pencils.
Some pencils are erasers.

Conclusions:
I. Some pens are erasers.
II. Some erasers are pencils.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: All + Some gives no definite link between the end terms; 'some' converts
solution.explanation: The pencils that are erasers need not be pens, so I does not follow. 'Some pencils are erasers' converts to 'Some erasers are pencils', so II follows.
steps: All pens are pencils, Some pencils are erasers: the middle term 'pencils' is not fully covered in the 'some' statement, so no pen–eraser link is certain
I: not definite (pens may lie outside the eraser part of pencils)
II: conversion of 'Some pencils are erasers' gives 'Some erasers are pencils': follows
solution.shortcut: All + Some = no conclusion between the end terms.
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I is the classic trap: the 'some' part of pencils may not include any pen.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:

No folder is a drawer.

Conclusions:
I. Some files are not drawers.
II. No file is a drawer.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: The files that are folders cannot be drawers, so some files are definitely not drawers (I follows). Other files may still be drawers, so 'No file is a drawer' is not certain.
steps: Some files are folders; no folder is a drawer
Those files that are folders are not drawers ⇒ Some files are not drawers: I follows
Files outside 'folders' are unrestricted, so some files could be drawers: II does not follow
solution.shortcut: Some + No ⇒ Some-not (first term to third term).
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

I. All coins are cheques.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: All + All = All; 'All' implies 'Some' in reverse
solution.explanation: Coins lie inside notes, and notes inside cheques, so all coins are cheques (I). Since coins exist and all of them are cheques, some cheques are coins (II).
steps: All coins ⊂ notes ⊂ cheques ⇒ All coins are cheques: I follows
All coins are cheques ⇒ Some cheques are coins (conversion of 'All' gives 'Some'): II follows
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
No tree is a bush.
All bushes are shrubs.

Conclusions:
I. No tree is a shrub.
II. Some trees are shrubs.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.concept: Complementary pair: 'Some' and 'No' between the same two terms
solution.explanation: Neither conclusion is definite: trees are kept away only from bushes, and the shrubs outside 'bushes' may or may not include trees. But one of the two must be true, because either some tree is a shrub or none is. So either I or II follows.
steps: No tree is a bush; all bushes are shrubs ⇒ only 'Some shrubs are not trees' is certain
I (No tree is a shrub) is not certain; II (Some trees are shrubs) is not certain
I and II are about the same pair (trees, shrubs) and form a 'No' / 'Some' pair: exactly one must be true

II. R > O

Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: M > N ≥ O = P gives M > P. O = P < Q ≤ R gives R > O. Both follow.
steps: I: M > N ≥ O = P → the path has a strict '>' and no reversed sign: M > P, true
II: O = P < Q ≤ R → R > O, true

II: B < C = D ≥ E: '<' and '≥' point in opposite directions → no relation, not definite

II: K ≤ L < M → M > K, true

II: X ≤ W < V = U ≥ T: reverses at U → no relation

steps: I (E > C) alone is not certain; II (E = C) alone is not certain
Together they form E ≥ C, which is certain: Either I or II follows
solution.shortcut: When the derived sign is ≥ (or ≤) and the conclusions are the matching > and =, the answer is Either.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' here (four-option rule), since E > C and E = C cannot both be true.

I: P > Q ≥ R > S = U → P > U, true

I: M > N? Both M and N are only known to be above L: no relation
II: N > L = K > J → N > J, true

II: R > P: R > Q ≤ P → no relation

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Which of the following sets of symbols, filled in order in the blanks of the expression below, makes both 'P > T' and 'S ≥ R' definitely true?

solution.concept: Building an expression that forces given conclusions
solution.explanation: With ≥, >, =, ≥ the expression is P ≥ Q > R = S ≥ T. The path from P to T contains a strict '>' and no reversed sign, so P > T; and R = S gives S ≥ R. Every other option fails at least one conclusion.

Option '>, ≥, ≤, >': P > Q ≥ R ≤ S > T → reverses at R: P > T fails

I: I ≥ D > E ≥ F ≥ G = H → I > H (one strict sign), true
II: E ≥ F ≥ G = H → E ≥ H, true

Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Decoded: T ≤ U ≤ X, U > V = W > Y. T ≤ U ≤ X gives only T ≤ X, so T < X is not certain. Y and T are both below U but along different branches, so they cannot be compared.
steps: Decode: T ≤ U, U > V, V = W, X ≥ U, Y < W
T ≤ U ≤ X and U > V = W > Y
I: T < X? Only T ≤ X is certain (T = U = X possible): not definite
II: Y < T? T ≤ U and Y < W < U: both below U, no relation

solution.explanation: Combined: G ≥ B ≥ C > D ≥ E = F. The path from G to F contains the strict sign C > D, so G > F. D ≥ E = F gives D ≥ F. Both follow.
steps: Rewrite each statement in one direction: G ≥ B, B ≥ C, C > D, D ≥ E, E = F
Combined: G ≥ B ≥ C > D ≥ E = F
I: G > F (one strict sign, no reversal): true
II: D ≥ E = F → D ≥ F: true
solution.why_others_wrong: Students who stop at G ≥ B ≥ C often miss that C > D makes the G–F relation strict.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Pointing to a man, Neha said, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother." How is Neha related to the man?

solution.concept: Decoding a pointing statement from the speaker outward
solution.explanation: 'The only daughter of my mother' is Neha herself (a woman speaking about her own mother's only daughter). So the man's mother is Neha.
steps: Only daughter of Neha's mother = Neha
So Neha is the man's mother
solution.shortcut: When a woman says 'only daughter of my mother', it is herself.
solution.why_others_wrong: Sister or aunt would need the 'only daughter' to be someone other than Neha.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A is the brother of B. B is the daughter of C. D is the father of C. How is A related to D?

solution.explanation: A and B are siblings, so A is also C's child. D is C's father, so A, a male one generation below C, is D's grandson.
steps: A brother of B, B child of C ⇒ A is C's son
D is C's father ⇒ D is two generations above A

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ravi's father is Suresh. Suresh's sister is Kamla, and Kamla's husband is Mohan. How is Mohan related to Ravi?

solution.explanation: Kamla is Ravi's father's sister, i.e. his aunt; her husband Mohan is Ravi's uncle.
steps: Kamla → sister of Suresh → Ravi's aunt
Mohan → husband of Kamla → Ravi's uncle

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Decoding a coded relation chain left to right
solution.explanation: M is the son of N, and N is the wife of O, so M is O's son. O is the father of P, and P is the sister of Q, so Q is also O's child. M and Q are children of the same parents, and M is male: M is Q's brother.
steps: M ÷ N: M is the son of N
N × O: N is the wife of O ⇒ M is the son of O and N
O + P: O is the father of P; P − Q: P is the sister of Q ⇒ Q is also O's child
M (male) and Q share parents ⇒ M is Q's brother

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Introducing a woman, Arun said, "She is the wife of the only grandson of my father's father." How is the woman related to Arun?

solution.explanation: Arun is a grandson of his own father's father. If that man has only one grandson, it must be Arun himself. So the woman is the wife of Arun.
steps: My father's father = Arun's paternal grandfather
His only grandson = Arun (Arun is male and is his grandson)
Wife of that grandson = Arun's wife
solution.why_others_wrong: Sister-in-law would need the grandson to be Arun's brother, but the grandson is unique and Arun is himself a grandson.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
There are six members P, Q, R, S, T and U in a family of three generations, with two married couples.
- Q is the father-in-law of T.
- S is the grandmother of R.
- U is the sister of P.
- R is the son of T.
- Q is married to S, and P is the only son of Q.

How is U related to R?

solution.explanation: Q and S are the grandparents. P is their only son and is married to T (T is Q's daughter-in-law). R is the son of P and T. U is P's sister, so U is R's father's sister: his aunt.
steps: Q is T's father-in-law and P is Q's only son ⇒ T is P's wife
R is T's son ⇒ R is P's son; S (Q's wife) is R's grandmother
U is P's sister ⇒ U is R's paternal aunt

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.explanation: K is L's brother and L is M's daughter, so K is M's son. M is N's husband, so N is K's mother.
steps: K # L: K is the brother of L
L & M: L is the daughter of M ⇒ K is M's son
M $ N: M is the husband of N ⇒ N is the mother of K and L
N @ O: N is O's mother (not needed for the question)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A family of three generations has eight members: Harsh, Gita, Kunal, Lata, Meena, Naresh, Om and Pari. There are three married couples, and each couple of the second generation has exactly one child.
- Om is the grandson of Gita.
- Meena is the daughter-in-law of Harsh.
- Pari is the niece of Kunal.
- Naresh is the son-in-law of Gita.
- Lata is the sister of Kunal.
- Harsh is the husband of Gita, and they have only two children.
- Om is the son of Meena.

How is Om related to Lata?

solution.explanation: Harsh and Gita have two children, Kunal and Lata. Meena is Harsh's daughter-in-law, so she is Kunal's wife; Om is their son. Naresh is Gita's son-in-law, so he is Lata's husband, and Pari (Kunal's niece) is their daughter. Om is the son of Lata's brother: her nephew.
steps: Generation 1: Harsh + Gita; children: Kunal, Lata
Meena = Kunal's wife (daughter-in-law of Harsh); their son = Om
Naresh = Lata's husband (son-in-law of Gita); their daughter = Pari (Kunal's niece)
Om is the son of Lata's brother ⇒ nephew
solution.why_others_wrong: Cousin is Om's relation to Pari, not to Lata; grandson is his relation to Harsh and Gita.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.explanation: G is the father of H and I (H is I's sister). J is G's wife and I is J's son, so J is I's mother. K is J's mother, so K is I's maternal grandmother and I, a male, is K's grandson.
steps: G ★ H ● I: G is the father of H; H is the sister of I ⇒ G is I's father
J ▲ G and I ◆ J: J is G's wife and I's mother; I is male
K ■ J: K is J's mother
So K is I's grandmother and I is K's grandson

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a family of seven members of three generations — Bhanu, Chhaya, Dev, Esha, Farah, Gagan and Hina — there are two married couples.
- Hina is the granddaughter of Bhanu.
- Farah is the mother of Gagan.
- Esha is the only daughter of Chhaya.
- Dev is the son of Bhanu, and Bhanu has only one son.
- Gagan is the brother of Hina.
- Chhaya is the wife of Bhanu.
- Esha is unmarried.

How is Esha related to the mother of Gagan?

solution.explanation: Bhanu and Chhaya have two children, Dev and Esha. The grandchildren Gagan and Hina must be Dev's children (Esha is unmarried), so Farah is Dev's wife. Esha is the sister of Farah's husband: her sister-in-law.
steps: Generation 1: Bhanu + Chhaya; children Dev (only son) and Esha (only daughter)
Gagan and Hina are grandchildren of Bhanu; Esha is unmarried ⇒ they are Dev's children ⇒ Farah is Dev's wife
Esha = sister of Farah's husband ⇒ sister-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Aunt is Esha's relation to Gagan and Hina, not to their mother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ravi walks 10 m towards the north. He then turns right and walks 6 m, and then turns right again and walks 4 m. How far is he now from his starting point, and in which direction?

solution.explanation: Net movement: 6 m east and 10 − 4 = 6 m north. Distance = √(6² + 6²) = 6√2 m (about 8.49 m), towards the north-east of the start.
steps: Distance = √(36 + 36) = 6√2 m; x > 0 and y > 0 → North-East

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point A is 5 m west of point B. Point C is 8 m north of point B. Point D is 5 m east of point C. In which direction is point A with respect to point D?

solution.explanation: Taking B as (0, 0): A = (−5, 0), C = (0, 8), D = (5, 8). From D to A the move is 10 m west and 8 m south, so A is to the south-west of D.
steps: A − D = (−10, −8): west and south ⇒ South-West

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: One morning after sunrise, Neeraj was standing facing a pole. The shadow of the pole fell exactly to his right. Which direction was Neeraj facing?

solution.explanation: In the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows fall towards the west. The shadow is on Neeraj's right, so his right hand points west, which means he is facing south.
steps: Shadow on his right ⇒ his right = west
Facing south, the right hand points west ⇒ he faces South
solution.shortcut: Morning: shadow west. Whatever side the shadow is on tells you where that hand points.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Starting from her house, Kiran drives 7 km towards the east. She then turns left and drives 9 km, turns right and drives 5 km, and finally turns right and drives 4 km. What is the shortest distance between her house and her present position?

solution.explanation: East: 7 + 5 = 12 km. North: 9 − 4 = 5 km. Shortest distance = √(12² + 5²) = 13 km.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point P is 4 m south of point Q. Point R is 3 m east of point P. Point S is 7 m north of point R. Point T is 6 m west of point S. How far is point T from point Q, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Coordinates of a chain of points
solution.explanation: With Q at (0, 0): P = (0, −4), R = (3, −4), S = (3, 3), T = (−3, 3). T is 3 m west and 3 m north of Q: 3√2 m to the north-west.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: One evening before sunset, Asha and Bela were standing facing each other. Asha's shadow fell exactly to Bela's left. Which direction was Asha facing?

solution.concept: Shadows in the evening, two observers
solution.explanation: In the evening the sun is in the west, so shadows fall to the east. Asha's shadow is on Bela's left, so Bela's left points east and Bela faces south. Asha faces Bela, so Asha faces north.
steps: Bela's left = east ⇒ Bela faces south
Asha faces Bela ⇒ Asha faces north
solution.why_others_wrong: South is Bela's direction, not Asha's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A man is facing north-west. He turns 90° clockwise, then 180° anticlockwise, and then 135° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?

solution.explanation: Measure directions clockwise from north: north-west = 315°. 315 + 90 − 180 + 135 = 360°, i.e. north.
solution.shortcut: Net turn = 90 − 180 + 135 = 45° clockwise; north-west turned 45° clockwise is north.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.explanation: With Q at (0, 0): P = (0, 3), R = (4, 0), S = (4, −3), T = (0, −3). R − T = (4, 3), so R is 5 m from T, towards the north-east.
steps: R − T = (4, 3) → distance √(16 + 9) = 5 m; east and north of T → North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West is T's direction from R (the reverse).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point J is 6 m east of point K. Point L is 8 m north of point J. Point M is 12 m west of point L. Point N is 8 m south of point M. Point O is 3 m east of point N. Point P is 4 m north of point O. How far is point K from point P, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Long chain of points on a grid
steps: K − P = (3, −4) → √(9 + 16) = 5 m; east and south → South-East
solution.why_others_wrong: North-West is P's direction from K; 3 m is only the east–west gap.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Rohit and Sohan start from the same point X. Rohit walks 10 m east, turns left and walks 6 m, then turns left again and walks 4 m. Sohan walks 6 m west, then turns right and walks 15 m. What is the shortest distance between Rohit and Sohan now, and in which direction is Sohan with respect to Rohit?

solution.explanation: Rohit ends at (6, 6) and Sohan at (−6, 15). Sohan − Rohit = (−12, 9), so the distance is √(144 + 81) = 15 m and Sohan is to the north-west of Rohit.
steps: Difference (−12, 9) → 15 m; west and north → North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East is Rohit's direction from Sohan; 21 m adds the legs instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, MANGO is written as NBOHP. How is GRAPE written in that code language?

solution.explanation: Each letter of MANGO moves one place forward (M→N, A→B, N→O, G→H, O→P). Applying +1 to GRAPE gives HSBQF.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If CAT is coded as 24, how will DOG be coded in the same code?

solution.explanation: CAT = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24, so a word is coded as the sum of its letters' positions. DOG = 4 + 15 + 7 = 26.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BRANCH is written as IDOBSC. How is LOAN written in that code?

solution.explanation: Each letter of BRANCH is moved one place forward (CSBODI) and the result is written in reverse (IDOBSC). LOAN → MPBO → reversed OBPM.
solution.why_others_wrong: MPBO forgets the reversal.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'bank loan rate' is written as 'ka pi zo',
'loan is low' is written as 'zo mu re', and
'rate is high' is written as 'pi mu tu'.
What is the code for 'loan'?

solution.explanation: 'loan' appears in the first two sentences, and the only code common to them is 'zo'.
steps: Sentences 1 and 2 share the word 'loan' and the code 'zo'
(Also: rate = pi from sentences 1 and 3, is = mu from 2 and 3)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'save money now' is written as 'la ri ko',
'money grows fast' is written as 'ri tu pe',
'save time now' is written as 'ko sa la', and
'time grows slowly' is written as 'sa pe mi'.
What is the code for 'fast'?

solution.explanation: money = ri (sentences 1 and 2), grows = pe (sentences 2 and 4). The remaining code of sentence 2, 'tu', must be 'fast'.
steps: Sentence 2 = money grows fast = ri tu pe ⇒ fast = tu

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, LOCKER is written as OLXPVI. How is SAFETY written in that code?

solution.explanation: Each letter is replaced by its opposite in the alphabet (position p → 27 − p): L↔O, O↔L, C↔X, K↔P, E↔V, R↔I. SAFETY → HZUVGB.
steps: S→H, A→Z, F→U, E→V, T→G, Y→B
solution.shortcut: Opposite pairs to remember: A-Z, E-V, F-U, S-H, T-G, Y-B.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, PEARL is written as '11 22 26 9 15'. How is STONE written in that code?

solution.explanation: Each letter is coded by its position counted from Z (27 − position): P (16) → 11, E (5) → 22, A (1) → 26. For STONE: S → 8, T → 7, O → 12, N → 13, E → 22.
solution.why_others_wrong: '19 20 15 14 5' uses forward positions; the other two swap a pair of digits.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, CHAPTER is written as AHCPRET. How is DEPOSIT written in that code?

solution.concept: Reversing each half around the middle letter
solution.explanation: CHAPTER = CHA | P | TER; each three-letter half is reversed (AHC, RET) and the middle letter stays. DEPOSIT = DEP | O | SIT → PED O TIS = PEDOTIS.
steps: CHA → AHC, P stays, TER → RET (matches)
DEP → PED, O stays, SIT → TIS

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'credit card limit' is written as 'xo ve li',
'card fee waived' is written as 've ra qu',
'limit fee raised' is written as 'li ra ne', and
'credit score raised' is written as 'xo ne su'.
What does the code 'ra' stand for?

solution.concept: Decoding a code back to its word
solution.explanation: 'ra' appears in sentences 2 and 3, and the only word common to those sentences is 'fee'.
steps: Sentences 2 and 3 share the code 'ra' and the word 'fee'
(Also: card = ve, limit = li, raised = ne, credit = xo)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the letter codes and conditions below.

| Letter | A | D | E | G | K | M | P | R | T | U |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Code | 7 | % | 2 | @ | 5 | 9 | # | 4 | © | 8 |

Conditions (apply only the first one that fits):
(i) If the first letter is a vowel and the last letter is a consonant, the codes of the first and last letters are interchanged.
(ii) If the first letter is a consonant and the last letter is a vowel, both are coded as the code of the vowel.
(iii) If both the first and the last letters are consonants, both are coded as ★.

What is the code for the letter group PADKER?

solution.explanation: PADKER begins with P and ends with R, both consonants, so condition (iii) applies: both end letters become ★, and the middle letters keep their table codes (A 7, D %, K 5, E 2).
steps: First letter P (consonant), last letter R (consonant): condition (iii)
solution.why_others_wrong: '#7%524' ignores the conditions; '★7%5★2' places ★ on the wrong letter.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'risk free bond yield' is written as 'ga lo mi tu',
'bond yield rises' is written as 'mi tu ve',
'free credit offer' is written as 'lo pa ke', and
'credit risk rises' is written as 'pa ga ve'.
What is the code for 'risk offer'?

solution.concept: Multi-step elimination (codes may appear in any order)
solution.explanation: bond and yield take mi and tu (sentences 1 and 2), so rises = ve. free = lo (sentences 1 and 3), credit = pa (sentences 3 and 4), so risk = ga (the remaining code of sentence 4) and offer = ke (the remaining code of sentence 3). 'risk offer' = 'ga ke'.
steps: Sentence 4: credit pa, rises ve ⇒ risk = ga
Sentence 3: free lo, credit pa ⇒ offer = ke
solution.why_others_wrong: 'mi ke' fails because mi belongs to bond or yield, which cannot be told apart.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, each vowel of a word is replaced by the letter two places after it in the English alphabet, each consonant by the letter immediately before it, and the resulting letters are then written in reverse order. For example, BANK is written as JMCA. How is CLIENT written in that code?

solution.concept: Separate rules for vowels and consonants, then reversal
solution.explanation: C→B, L→K, I→K, E→G, N→M, T→S gives BKKGMS; reversing gives SMGKKB.
steps: Check BANK: B→A, A→C, N→M, K→J = ACMJ → reverse JMCA (matches)
CLIENT: consonants −1 (C→B, L→K, N→M, T→S); vowels +2 (I→K, E→G)
solution.why_others_wrong: BKKGMS skips the reversal; the other two mis-shift one letter.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, KITE is written as 5292: each letter is replaced by the digit sum of its alphabetical position (reduced to a single digit), and the digits are then written in reverse order. How is MOTOR written in that code?

solution.concept: Digit sums of positions, then reversal
steps: Check KITE: K 11 → 2, I 9, T 20 → 2, E 5 → 2925 → reverse 5292 (matches)
solution.why_others_wrong: 46269 skips the reversal.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

R 4 # M 7 K @ 2 P E 9 $ T 3 & B 5 W

Which element is 6th to the right of the 9th element from the left end?

solution.explanation: 6th to the right of the 9th from the left is the (9 + 6) = 15th element from the left: &.
steps: Counting 6 to the right: E, 9, $, T, 3, &
solution.shortcut: Same direction: add the positions (9 + 6 = 15 from the left).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

D 8 % L 3 Q © 6 A 1 ★ N 5 H 2 # Y 7

How many numbers in the arrangement are immediately preceded by a letter?

solution.explanation: Look at every number and check the element just before it: D 8, L 3, A 1, N 5, H 2, Y 7. That is 6.
steps: List each number with the element before it
Keep the pairs where the earlier element is a letter
Pairs: D8; L3; A1; N5; H2; Y7

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

H 3 % K 8 R © 1 A 6 # Z D 4 ★ U 9 M @ 2 F E 7 $ G

How many symbols in the arrangement are immediately preceded by a number and immediately followed by a letter?

solution.explanation: Qualifying triplets (number, symbol, letter): 3 % K; 6 # Z; 4 ★ U; 7 $ G. Total 4.
steps: Keep those with a number before and a letter after

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

5 B @ T 9 E 2 # K M 6 & 1 R I ★ 8 S $ 3 L A 4 % W

If all the symbols are removed from the arrangement, which element will be 5th to the left of the 14th element from the left end?

solution.explanation: Without symbols the series is: 5 B T 9 E 2 K M 6 1 R I 8 S 3 L A 4 W. 5th to the left of the 14th element is the (14 − 5) = 9th element: 6.
steps: New series: 5 B T 9 E 2 K M 6 1 R I 8 S 3 L A 4 W
solution.why_others_wrong: K is the 9th element of the original series (symbols not removed); W is 5th to the right of the 14th; M is an off-by-one count.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

J 7 E 4 @ U 2 Q # O 8 V I 1 & S 6 A $ 9 C ★ 5 G

How many vowels in the arrangement are immediately followed by a number?

solution.explanation: Vowels followed by a number: E 4; U 2; O 8; I 1. Total 4.
steps: Vowels present: E, U, O, I, A

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

B 4 $ R 9 E K @ 2 W 6 # A M 1 % Y 8 I © T 3 F 5 ★ N

If the first thirteen elements of the arrangement are written in reverse order, which element will be 8th to the right of the 5th element from the left end?

solution.explanation: After reversing the first 13 elements the series begins A # 6 W 2 @ K E 9 R $ 4 B M 1 … The 5th + 8 = 13th element is B.
steps: First 13 reversed: A # 6 W 2 @ K E 9 R $ 4 B
Rest unchanged: M 1 % Y 8 I © T 3 F 5 ★ N
13th element of the new series = B
solution.why_others_wrong: In the new series @, R and Y are the 6th, 10th and 17th elements, so they come from miscounting; without the reversal the 13th element would be A.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

8 @ 3 G % 6 7 K # 2 4 © P 5 ★ 9 1 $ Q 6 & 3 D

How many even numbers in the arrangement are immediately preceded by a symbol and immediately followed by an odd number?

solution.explanation: Triplets (symbol, even number, odd number): % 6 7. Total 1.
steps: Check the element before (symbol?) and after (odd number?)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which letter is 7th to the right of the 15th letter from the left end of the English alphabet?

solution.explanation: 7th to the right of the 15th letter is the (15 + 7) = 22nd letter: V.
solution.shortcut: Remember E-J-O-T-Y = 5-10-15-20-25; 22 is two after T.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many pairs of letters are there in the word 'GARDEN' each of which has as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (counting both forward and backward)?

solution.concept: Comparing word gaps with alphabet gaps
solution.explanation: Pairs found: GD, DE. Total 2.
steps: Positions: G = 7, A = 1, R = 18, D = 4, E = 5, N = 14
For each pair, compare the gap in the word with the gap in the alphabet

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the English alphabet is written in reverse order (Z to A), which letter will be 6th to the right of the 11th letter from the left end?

solution.explanation: In the reversed alphabet the k-th letter from the left is the (27 − k)-th letter of the normal alphabet. 11 + 6 = 17th from the left → 27 − 17 = 10th normal letter: J.
steps: Reversed alphabet: Z Y X W V U T S R Q P O N M L K J …
11th from left = P; 6 more to the right → 17th
17th from left in the reversed alphabet = J
solution.why_others_wrong: Q is the result of using the normal alphabet (17th letter).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If a meaningful English word is formed using the 1st, 2nd, 5th and 6th letters of the word 'MAGNETIC', each letter used exactly once, what is the first letter of that word? If no such word can be formed, choose 'No such word can be formed'; if more than one such word can be formed, choose 'More than one such word can be formed'.

options.text: No such word can be formed
More than one such word can be formed

solution.concept: Picking letters by position, then forming words
solution.explanation: The letters are M, A, E and T. They form several words: MATE, MEAT, TEAM and TAME. So more than one word can be formed.
solution.why_others_wrong: M and T are first letters of some of the words, but there is no single word.
solution.final_answer: Option D: More than one such word can be formed

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many pairs of letters are there in the word 'TRANSPORT' each of which has as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (counting both forward and backward)?

solution.concept: Exhaustive pair checking in a longer word
solution.explanation: Pairs found: NP, NR, PO, PR. Total 4.
steps: Check every pair (i, j): |alphabet gap| must equal j − i
Matching pairs: N–P, N–R, P–O, P–R

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the word 'EDUCATION', each vowel is replaced by the letter immediately after it in the English alphabet and each consonant by the letter immediately before it. The new letters are then arranged in alphabetical order from left to right. Which letter will be 3rd from the right end?

solution.concept: Transform, sort, then count from the right
solution.explanation: The new letters are F C V B B S J P M; in alphabetical order B B C F J M P S V. The 3rd from the right is P.
steps: E→F, D→C, U→V, C→B, A→B, T→S, I→J, O→P, N→M
New letters: F C V B B S J P M
Sorted: B B C F J M P S V

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following five numbers:
742   319   865   427   583

If the first and the third digits of each number are interchanged, which number will become the largest?

solution.explanation: After interchange: 742 → 247, 319 → 913, 865 → 568, 427 → 724, 583 → 385. The largest new number is 913, which comes from 319.
solution.why_others_wrong: 865 is the largest before the interchange.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following five numbers:
476   813   592   368   735

If 1 is added to the first digit of each number and 1 is subtracted from its last digit, how many of the new numbers will be divisible by 3?

solution.concept: Digit operations and the divisibility rule for 3
solution.explanation: New numbers: 575, 912, 691, 467, 834. A number is divisible by 3 when its digit sum is. 575: 17; 912: 12; 691: 16; 467: 17; 834: 15. So 2 are divisible by 3.
solution.shortcut: The operation does not change the digit sum (+1 and −1), so test the original numbers.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following five numbers:
518   364   927   285   619

If the digits within each number are arranged in descending order, what is the difference between the second highest and the lowest of the new numbers?

solution.explanation: New numbers: 518 → 851, 364 → 643, 927 → 972, 285 → 852, 619 → 961. Second highest = 961, lowest = 643; difference = 318.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following five numbers:
638   471   925   362   814

If the second and third digits of each number are interchanged and the new numbers are arranged in ascending order, what is the product of the first and last digits of the number in the middle?

solution.why_others_wrong: 48 comes from the original middle number 638 (no interchange); 28 and 8 come from taking 417 or 841 as the middle number.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a row of 40 students facing north, Meena is 14th from the left end and Raju is 20th from the right end. How many students sit between Meena and Raju?

solution.concept: Converting a right-end rank to a left-end rank
solution.explanation: Raju's position from the left = 40 − 20 + 1 = 21. Between positions 14 and 21 there are 6 students.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Arjun ranks 9th from the top and 32nd from the bottom in his class. How many students are there in the class?

solution.concept: Total = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1
solution.explanation: Arjun is counted in both ranks, so the class has 9 + 32 − 1 = 40 students.
solution.why_others_wrong: 41 counts Arjun twice.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a queue, Amit is 12th from the front and Bala is 18th from the back. If they interchange their positions, Amit becomes 22nd from the front. How many people are there in the queue?

solution.explanation: After interchange Amit stands where Bala stood, so Bala's position was 22nd from the front and 18th from the back. Total = 22 + 18 − 1 = 39.
steps: Bala's place = 22nd from front (Amit's new place)
solution.why_others_wrong: 33 uses Amit's old position (12 + 22 − 1).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T and U have different weights. P is heavier than Q but lighter than U. R is lighter than Q but heavier than T. S is the lightest.

Which box is the third heaviest?

solution.explanation: U > P > Q and Q > R > T join into U > P > Q > R > T, with S lightest. The third heaviest is Q.
steps: Combined: U > P > Q > R > T > S

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Some persons sit in a row facing north. Pankaj is 7th from the left end. Qureshi sits 5th to the right of Pankaj. Rana sits immediately to the right of Qureshi and is 9th from the right end. Sumit sits exactly in the middle of the row. How many persons sit between Sumit and Rana?

solution.concept: Unknown row length from overlapping ranks
solution.explanation: Qureshi = 7 + 5 = 12th, Rana = 13th from the left. Rana is 9th from the right, so the row has 13 + 9 − 1 = 21 persons. The middle seat is 11th, and between seat 11 and seat 13 there is 1 person.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Nikhil, Oorja, Prem, Ritika, Shaan and Trisha have different weights, each a whole number of kilograms.
- Prem is heavier than only two persons.
- Ritika is heavier than Prem but lighter than Shaan.
- Nikhil is lighter than Oorja, and Oorja is heavier than Ritika.
- Trisha is the lightest, and Oorja is not the heaviest.
- The heaviest person weighs 82 kg and the lightest 48 kg.
- Ritika weighs 67 kg and Nikhil 55 kg.

What is the minimum possible combined weight of Oorja and Prem?

solution.concept: Ordering, then the tightest integer bounds
solution.explanation: The order is Shaan > Oorja > Ritika > Prem > Nikhil > Trisha. Oorja must be above Ritika (67), so at least 68 kg; Prem must be above Nikhil (55), so at least 56 kg. Minimum total = 68 + 56 = 124 kg.
steps: Prem has exactly two persons lighter: Trisha (lightest) and one more
Ritika > Prem and Oorja > Ritika, Nikhil < Oorja: the only person who can be below Prem besides Trisha is Nikhil
Ritika, Oorja and Shaan take the top three places with Ritika lowest; Oorja is not the heaviest, so Shaan is
Order: Shaan 82 > Oorja > Ritika 67 > Prem > Nikhil 55 > Trisha 48
solution.why_others_wrong: 122 kg uses 67 and 55 themselves, but weights are all different.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A word arrangement machine rearranges a line of words step by step. In each step it takes the word that comes earliest in alphabetical order among the words not yet arranged and moves it to the immediate right of the words already arranged (in Step I, to the extreme left). The other words keep their order.

Input: sun bat ink cot apex dew

In which step will the arrangement read 'apex bat cot sun ink dew'?

solution.explanation: Each step fixes the next word in alphabetical order at the left. After three steps apex, bat and cot are in place, giving 'apex bat cot sun ink dew'.
steps: Step I: apex sun bat ink cot dew
Step II: apex bat sun ink cot dew
Step III: apex bat cot sun ink dew
Step IV: apex bat cot dew sun ink
Step V: apex bat cot dew ink sun

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A number arrangement machine rearranges numbers step by step. In each step it takes the largest number among those not yet arranged and moves it to the immediate right of the numbers already arranged (in Step I, to the extreme left). The other numbers keep their order.

Input: 34 89 12 57 76 41

Which number is 3rd from the right end in Step III?

solution.explanation: Step I: 89 34 12 57 76 41; Step II: 89 76 34 12 57 41; Step III: 89 76 57 34 12 41. The 3rd from the right in Step III is 34.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many steps are needed to complete the arrangement of the given input?

solution.concept: Simulating a two-rule machine step by step
solution.explanation: There are five numbers and five words, and each step arranges one of each, so 5 steps are needed (Step V is the last).
steps: Step I: 17 lamp 52 opal gate 64 kite 39 85 brick
Step II: 39 17 lamp 52 opal 64 kite 85 brick gate
Step III: 52 39 17 lamp opal 64 85 brick gate kite
Step IV: 64 52 39 17 opal 85 brick gate kite lamp
Step V: 85 64 52 39 17 brick gate kite lamp opal

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In Step II, which element is 3rd to the right of 'kite'?

solution.concept: Simulating a two-rule machine step by step
solution.explanation: Step II is '39 17 lamp 52 opal 64 kite 85 brick gate'. Counting three places to the right of 'kite' gives 'gate'.
steps: Step I: 17 lamp 52 opal gate 64 kite 39 85 brick
Step II: 39 17 lamp 52 opal 64 kite 85 brick gate

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the last step, which two elements are 5th and 6th from the left end?

solution.concept: Simulating a two-rule machine step by step
solution.explanation: The last step is '85 64 52 39 17 brick gate kite lamp opal'. Its 5th and 6th elements are 17 and brick.
steps: Step V: 85 64 52 39 17 brick gate kite lamp opal

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A machine rearranges words step by step. In each step it takes, among the words not yet arranged, the word with the most letters (if two words are equally long, the one that comes first in alphabetical order), changes its first letter to the next letter of the alphabet, and places it immediately to the right of the words already arranged (in Step I, at the extreme left). The other words keep their order.

Input: mint orbit cask fern quilt pasture

Which word will be 5th from the left end in Step IV?

solution.concept: Selection by length, with a transformation
solution.explanation: Order of selection: pasture (7), orbit (5), quilt (5), cask (4), fern (4), mint (4) — ties broken alphabetically. Step IV is 'qasture prbit ruilt dask mint fern', whose 5th word is mint.
steps: Step I: qasture mint orbit cask fern quilt
Step II: qasture prbit mint cask fern quilt
Step III: qasture prbit ruilt mint cask fern
Step IV: qasture prbit ruilt dask mint fern
Step V: qasture prbit ruilt dask gern mint
Step VI: qasture prbit ruilt dask gern nint
solution.why_others_wrong: quilt has already become 'ruilt' and moved left by Step III; 'nint' is mint after it is picked, which happens only in Step VI.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A machine rearranges numbers step by step. In each step it takes the largest number not yet arranged, reverses its digits and places it immediately to the right of the numbers already placed at the left end (in Step I, at the extreme left). In the same step it takes the smallest number not yet arranged, adds 5 to it and places it immediately to the left of the numbers already placed at the right end (in Step I, at the extreme right). The remaining numbers keep their order in the middle.

Input: 47 81 26 93 58 34

What is the sum of the two numbers at the extreme ends in Step II?

solution.explanation: Step I: 39 47 81 58 34 31. Step II: 39 18 47 58 39 31. Ends of Step II: 39 and 31; sum = 70.
solution.shortcut: The left end never changes after Step I (39 from 93), and in Step II the right end is the second smallest number + 5 placed to the left of 31, so the extreme right stays 31.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Among P, Q, R, S and T, each of a different height, who is the tallest?

I. S is taller than P, and P is taller than both Q and R.
II. T is shorter than Q.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: I alone leaves T unplaced, so S or T could be the tallest. II alone says nothing about P, R or S. Together, T is below Q, which is below P and S, so S is the tallest.
steps: I: S > P > Q, P > R; T unknown → tallest is S or T: not sufficient
II: T < Q only: not sufficient
I + II: S > P > Q > T and P > R → S is tallest: sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: In which direction is village M with respect to village N?

I. Village M is 4 km east of village P, and village P is 4 km south of village N.
II. Village N is to the north-west of village M.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: From I, M is 4 km east and 4 km south of N, i.e. south-east. From II, if N is north-west of M then M is south-east of N. Each statement alone answers the question.
steps: I: N (0, 0) → P (0, −4) → M (4, −4): M is South-East of N: sufficient
II: N is North-West of M ⇒ M is South-East of N: sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option C: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F sit in a row facing north. Who sits at the extreme right end?

I. C sits third from the left end, and exactly two persons sit between C and E.
II. B sits immediately to the left of E, and F sits at the extreme left end.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: From I, C is at seat 3 and E, three seats away, must be at seat 6 (seat 0 does not exist): E is at the right end. II fixes only F and the B–E pair, which can sit in several places.
steps: I: C = 3; E = 3 ± 3 → E = 6 ⇒ E sits at the extreme right: sufficient
II: F = 1; B–E adjacent anywhere from seats 2–3 to 5–6: not sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: In a certain code language, what is the code for 'gold'?

I. 'gold rate rise' is written as 'tu ka pa', and 'rate cut now' is written as 'ka zi me'.
II. 'gold coin rise' is written as 'pa ro tu', and 'coin now sale' is written as 'ro me lo'.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.explanation: In every statement, and even when both are combined, 'gold' and 'rise' always appear together and share the codes 'tu' and 'pa'. Nothing separates them, so the code for 'gold' cannot be fixed.
steps: I: gold and rise ↔ {tu, pa} (rate = ka): not sufficient
II: gold and rise ↔ {pa, tu} (coin = ro): not sufficient
I + II: gold and rise still appear only together with {tu, pa}: not sufficient
Even together the statements are not sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statements I and II together are not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: On which day of the week did Mohan visit the bank?

I. Mohan did not visit the bank on a Saturday or a Sunday, and he visited after Wednesday.
II. Mohan visited the bank on the day after his brother did, and his brother visited after Tuesday but before Thursday.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: I leaves Thursday and Friday open. From II, the brother visited on Wednesday, so Mohan visited on Thursday.
steps: I: after Wednesday and not on a weekend → Thursday or Friday: not sufficient
II: brother on Wednesday (after Tuesday, before Thursday) → Mohan on Thursday: sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Among P, Q, R, S and T, each of a different age, who is the oldest?

I. P is older than both Q and R.
II. S is older than P.
III. T is younger than Q.

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
Only statements I and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Three-statement data sufficiency: test every pair before using all three
solution.explanation: No single statement or pair is enough: I + II leaves T unplaced; I + III leaves S unplaced; II + III leaves Q and R free. With all three, S > P > Q > T and P > R, so S is the oldest.
steps: I + II: S > P > Q, R; T could be older than S: not sufficient
I + III: P > Q > T, P > R; S unknown: not sufficient
II + III: S > P, Q > T; Q or R could be oldest: not sufficient
I + II + III: S > P > Q > T and P > R ⇒ S oldest: all three are necessary
solution.final_answer: Option C: All three statements I, II and III together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, equally spaced and facing the centre. Who sits opposite A?

I. C sits second to the left of A.
II. D is an immediate neighbour of both C and F.
III. B sits immediately to the right of A.

options.text: Only statements I and II together are sufficient
Only statements II and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient

solution.concept: Three-statement data sufficiency with a circular arrangement
solution.explanation: With I, C is two seats to A's left, which is next to the seat opposite A. II then needs D between C and F: D cannot sit on the side towards A (F would have to take A's seat), so D sits opposite A. So I and II together answer the question. III only places B next to A and does not complete any other combination.
steps: Number the seats 0–5 to A's right (A = 0, opposite A = 3)
I: C = 4. II alone: no fixed seat. III: B = 1
I + II: D beside C → seat 3 or 5; D = 5 would need F at seat 0 (A's seat), so D = 3: sufficient
I + III: C = 4, B = 1; seats 2, 3, 5 open for D, E, F: not sufficient
II + III: B = 1 and a C–D–F block elsewhere: not sufficient
Only I and II together are sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only statements I and II together are sufficient

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: A bank has announced that customers who register their mobile numbers with their accounts before 31 March will receive a free cheque book.

Assumptions:
I. Some customers would like a free cheque book enough to register their mobile numbers for it.
II. All customers of the bank have already registered their mobile numbers.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: An incentive is offered only if the bank believes it will motivate at least some customers, so I is implicit. II contradicts the very purpose of the offer: if everyone had already registered, no incentive would be needed.
steps: I: the offer makes sense only if a free cheque book attracts some customers: implicit
II: if all had registered, the offer would be pointless: not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Both or II fail because II goes against the reason for the announcement.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only assumption I is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: Notice in a bank branch: "Please collect a token from the token machine to avoid waiting in a long queue."

Assumptions:
I. Using the token machine reduces the time customers spend waiting in a queue.
II. Customers visiting the branch can read and act on the notice.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The notice promises less waiting through tokens, so I is assumed. Any written notice assumes its readers can read and follow it, so II is also assumed.
steps: I: the notice links tokens with avoiding a long queue: implicit
II: a notice is put up only if people are expected to read and act on it: implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I or Only II ignores one of the two things the notice takes for granted.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: The company has decided to shift its head office from Mumbai to Pune from next year.

Assumptions:
I. Pune offers a larger market for the company's products than Mumbai.
II. All the employees working at the head office will move to Pune with it.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: A head office can move for many reasons, such as lower rent or better talent, so a bigger market in Pune is not taken for granted. The decision also does not depend on every employee moving; some may resign or be replaced.
steps: I: the move could be for cost or other reasons; a larger market is not necessary: not implicit
II: the company need not assume 100% of staff will relocate: not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I reads a motive into the decision that the statement never needs.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: To reduce the cost of handling cash, a bank plans to install cash-recycler machines in its 200 busiest branches.

Assumptions:
I. Cash-recycler machines can lower the bank's cost of handling cash.
II. The 200 busiest branches handle a significant amount of cash.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The plan is meant to cut cash-handling cost, so the bank assumes the machines can do that (I). It picks the busiest branches because that is where enough cash is handled for the saving to matter (II).
steps: I: the stated goal is cost reduction through the machines: implicit
II: choosing the busiest branches for a cash-cost measure assumes they handle a lot of cash: implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I misses the reason for choosing these particular branches.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: The regulator has directed all lenders to display the annualised interest rate, including all fees, prominently in every loan advertisement.

Assumptions:
I. Borrowers can compare loan offers better when the full annualised cost is shown prominently.
II. Lenders have so far been charging interest above the legal limit.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The directive is about disclosure: it assumes that showing the full cost helps borrowers compare offers (I). It does not assume that any lender broke an interest-rate limit (II); a disclosure rule would not fix that anyway.
steps: I: the purpose of mandatory prominent disclosure is better comparison: implicit
II: the directive concerns how costs are shown, not whether rates are illegal: not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: II is a tempting 'reason' for regulation, but the statement neither needs nor implies it.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only assumption I is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: "Since our app now lets customers open a fixed deposit in three minutes, we expect deposits from young professionals to rise," said the bank's digital head.

Assumptions:
I. Young professionals have avoided opening fixed deposits only because the process was lengthy.
II. Young professionals value speed and convenience when choosing financial products.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The expectation rests on young professionals caring about speed and convenience (II). It does not need the lengthy process to have been the only reason they stayed away; 'only' makes I too strong.
steps: II: expecting more deposits from a faster process assumes the target group values speed: implicit
I: the speaker needs speed to be one factor, not the sole factor: 'only' makes it not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Both fails because of the word 'only' in I.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only assumption II is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: All candidates who score at least 60% in the written test will be called for the interview. Rahul scored 72% in the written test.

Conclusions:
I. Rahul will be called for the interview.
II. Rahul will be selected for the job.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Rahul meets the stated condition (72% ≥ 60%), so he will be called (I follows). Being called for an interview does not mean being selected (II does not follow).
steps: Selection depends on the interview, about which nothing is said: II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Both treats an interview call as selection.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: Every savings account in Bank X earns 3% interest a year, and every fixed deposit in Bank X earns at least 6% a year.

Conclusions:
I. A fixed deposit in Bank X earns more interest in a year than a savings account in Bank X with the same amount.
II. No fixed deposit in Bank X earns less than 6% a year.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: For equal amounts, a rate of at least 6% always beats 3%, so I follows. II simply restates 'at least 6%', so it follows too.
steps: I: FD rate ≥ 6% > 3% savings rate ⇒ more interest on the same amount: follows
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II overlooks that equal amounts make the rate comparison decisive.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The number of digital payment transactions in the country doubled last year, while the number of ATM cash withdrawals fell by 5%.

Conclusions:
I. People in the country have stopped using cash.
II. The number of digital payment transactions will double again this year.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: ATM withdrawals fell by only 5%, so cash is clearly still used (I fails). Last year's growth says nothing certain about this year's (II is a prediction, not a conclusion).
steps: I: a 5% fall in withdrawals means cash use continues: does not follow
II: a future growth rate cannot be concluded from one past year: does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I exaggerates a small fall into a complete stop.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: A survey of 2,000 small shop owners in five cities found that 64% of them accept payments through QR codes.

Conclusions:
I. Among the shop owners surveyed, those who accept QR-code payments outnumber those who do not.
II. 64% of all small shop owners in the country accept QR-code payments.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: 64% of the surveyed owners accept QR payments and 36% do not, so I follows. The survey covered five cities only; the figure cannot be extended to the whole country (II fails).
steps: I: 64% versus 36% within the sample: follows
II: a five-city sample does not establish a national percentage: does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Both generalises a sample to the whole population.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The state's tax collections in the first half of the year were higher than budgeted. Citing this, the state government has announced that it will meet this year's fiscal deficit target without cutting capital expenditure.

Conclusions:
I. The state government does not plan to cut capital expenditure in order to meet this year's fiscal deficit target.
II. The state's tax collections for the full year will be higher than budgeted.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: I restates the announced plan, so it follows. The statement covers only the first half of the year; the full-year collections may still fall short, so II does not follow.
steps: I: 'without cutting capital expenditure' is the announced plan: follows
II: first-half collections do not fix full-year collections: does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Both extends a half-year fact to the whole year.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: In a city, every bank branch that opened after 2020 has a solar rooftop. None of the branches of Bank Y in the city has a solar rooftop.

Conclusions:
I. Bank Y has no branches in the city.
II. No branch of Bank Y in the city opened after 2020.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: If any Bank Y branch had opened after 2020, it would have a solar rooftop, but none does; so none opened after 2020 (II). The statement refers to Bank Y's branches in the city, so it does not say they do not exist (I fails).
steps: Bank Y branches: no solar rooftop ⇒ not opened after 2020 (contrapositive): II follows
I is not implied: the statement speaks of Bank Y's branches in the city and gives no reason to think there are none: does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I misreads 'none of the branches has a rooftop' as 'there are no branches'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. Heavy unseasonal rain damaged the standing wheat crop in several districts of the state last week.
II. Wheat prices in the wholesale markets of the state rose sharply this week.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Crop damage reduces the expected supply of wheat, which pushes wholesale prices up. I came first and explains II, so I is the cause and II its effect.
steps: I (crop damage) happened before II (price rise)
Lower supply → higher prices: I explains II
So I is the cause and II the effect
solution.why_others_wrong: II cannot cause I: a price rise does not damage crops.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. Most IT firms in the city asked their employees to work from home on Monday.
II. All schools in the city remained closed on Monday.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Neither event causes the other: offices do not shut schools, and school closures do not make firms switch to work from home. Both are typical responses to one trigger, such as a severe weather warning or a city-wide shutdown on that day. So both are effects of a common cause.
steps: No direct link between I and II in either direction
Both are same-day precautionary measures of the kind taken after a single city-wide trigger
So both are effects of some common cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Effects of independent causes would fit only if the two closures had unrelated triggers, which the identical timing and scope make unlikely.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. The bank has extended its branch working hours to 7 pm on weekdays.
II. A survey by the bank showed that most of its salaried customers could not visit a branch before 5 pm.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: The survey finding (II) explains the decision to keep branches open later (I). II is the cause and I its effect.
steps: II reports a problem: customers cannot come before 5 pm
I is the bank's response: longer hours
So II is the cause and I the effect
solution.why_others_wrong: I cannot cause II: extending hours does not create the survey finding.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. The central bank kept its policy interest rate unchanged at its latest meeting.
II. Sales of air-conditioners rose sharply in the northern states this month.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Each statement is an outcome: the rate decision follows from the central bank's view of inflation and growth, and the jump in air-conditioner sales from hot weather and seasonal demand. Neither explains the other, and no single event explains both. So they are effects of independent causes.
steps: I is a decision (an effect of the monetary-policy assessment)
II is a market outcome (an effect of seasonal heat and demand)
No link between them and no shared trigger: effects of independent causes
solution.why_others_wrong: A common cause would need one event driving both a policy decision and a seasonal sales rise; nothing points to one.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Several customers of a bank branch have complained that its ATM often runs out of cash on weekends.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action for the bank?

options.text: Shut down the ATM on weekends so that customers stop complaining
Schedule an additional cash refill for the ATM before every weekend
Fine customers who withdraw cash from the ATM on weekends
Transfer the branch manager to another branch immediately

solution.concept: A course of action should solve the stated problem practically
solution.explanation: The problem is a cash shortage on weekends; an extra refill before weekends removes it directly.
steps: Identify the problem: the ATM runs dry on weekends
Choose the action that fixes the cause: more cash before the weekend
solution.why_others_wrong: Shutting the ATM or fining customers punishes users instead of solving the problem; transferring the manager does not put cash in the machine.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Schedule an additional cash refill for the ATM before every weekend

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a town, the number of two-wheeler loans sanctioned by banks in October was 30% higher than in September, while the number of two-wheeler loan applications was only 10% higher.

Which of the following can be inferred from this information?

options.text: A larger share of the applications was sanctioned in October than in September
Every application received in October was sanctioned
Banks lowered their interest rates on two-wheeler loans in October
More two-wheelers were sold in October than in any other month of the year

solution.concept: Inference must follow from the numbers given
solution.explanation: If sanctions grew by 30% and applications by only 10%, the ratio sanctions ÷ applications rose (1.3 ÷ 1.1 > 1). So a larger share of applications was approved in October.
steps: Sanction ratio in October = 1.30 S ÷ 1.10 A = 1.18 × (S ÷ A)
So the approval share rose by about 18%
No other option is supported by the data
solution.why_others_wrong: Interest rates and sales across the year are not mentioned; 'every application' is far stronger than the data.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A larger share of the applications was sanctioned in October than in September

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A coaching institute claims that its students do better in the bank PO exam than other candidates because of its weekly mock tests.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the institute's claim?

options.text: Some students of other institutes also clear the PO exam
The institute has branches in ten cities
The institute admits only students who have already scored highly in its own screening test
The institute's mock tests follow the latest exam pattern

solution.concept: Weakening a causal claim: find another explanation for the result
solution.explanation: If the institute admits only students who were already strong, their better results may come from that selection rather than from the mock tests, which undercuts the claimed cause.
steps: A weakener offers another cause for the better results
Pre-selecting strong students is such an alternative cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Following the latest pattern supports the claim; other institutes' successes and the number of branches do not touch the cause of this institute's results.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The institute admits only students who have already scored highly in its own screening test

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The city should build a flyover at the Station Road junction, because it will reduce the time commuters spend waiting in traffic there.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: A traffic study found that most vehicles at the junction go straight through it, which is the movement a flyover would carry
Some shopkeepers near the junction oppose the flyover
The city has already built two flyovers elsewhere
The flyover will take three years to build

solution.concept: Strengthening: show that the proposed means will produce the claimed effect
solution.explanation: A flyover only saves time for traffic that uses it. If most vehicles go straight through the junction, most of the traffic will bypass the signal, so waiting time falls: this supports the argument.
steps: Claim: flyover → less waiting at the junction
The claim depends on enough traffic using the flyover
Most vehicles going straight confirms that dependence
solution.why_others_wrong: Construction time and shopkeepers' views concern cost or opinion, not the time saved; flyovers elsewhere say nothing about this junction.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A traffic study found that most vehicles at the junction go straight through it, which is the movement a flyover would carry

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A bank's net profit equals its interest income plus other income, minus operating expenses, provisions for bad loans and tax. This year, Bank A's net profit rose by 20%, although its interest income, operating expenses and tax paid were all exactly the same as last year.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: Bank A gave out more loans this year than last year
Bank A's provisions for bad loans fell this year
Bank A's other income rose, or its provisions for bad loans fell, or both
Bank A's share price rose by 20% this year

solution.explanation: Profit rose while interest income, expenses and tax were unchanged. The only remaining items in the definition are other income (added) and provisions (subtracted), so at least one of them must have moved in profit's favour. Either alone could explain the rise, so only the combined statement must be true.
steps: Profit = interest income + other income − expenses − provisions − tax
